title: Lampard 'somewhere in the middle' of Mourinho and Ancelotti
description: Eight years into his own managerial career, Coventry City boss Frank Lampard cites Jose Mourinho and Carli Ancelotti as the main influences on his style.
fullText:
The Football Interview will be available on BBC One at 12:45 every Saturday during the Premier League season, as well as on BBC iPlayer, BBC Football YouTube and the BBC Sport website and app.

In the second episode of the new season, available on Saturday, 29 August, musician Tom Grennan sits down with Coventry City manager Frank Lampard.

As a player, Frank Lampard worked under some of the biggest managers in the game, including Jose Mourinho, Carlo Ancelotti, Guus Hiddink and Rafael Benitez - not to mention his uncle Harry Redknapp.

Eight years into his own managerial career, the Coventry City boss cited Mourinho and Ancelotti as the main influences on his style.

"Jose and Carlo are like both sides of the coin," the 48-year-old told BBC Sport.

"Jose was very on you, he transmitted his self-confidence, but if you stepped out of line or did something wrong, you'd feel the strength of him, whereas Carlo was chilled and calm. When you look back, you go, 'that's a nice environment to work in'. It felt like he trusted you. So I try and take little snippets. I'm probably somewhere in the middle."

Lampard played under Mourinho and Ancelotti at Chelsea and won the Premier League and FA Cup with them both.

He said it is important to strike a balance between the pair as he targets more success with Coventry.

"I start to sometimes go towards being Jose, sometimes I go and be a bit more Carlo," he added.

"I've learnt that young managers, you come in and feel like you have to to criticise a bad performance or say something about an individual that turns up late. The more I've done this job, I realise that they're all humans.

"Sometimes a lad comes in late, you don't know the back story. And so trying to jump on him and being this hard man manager, you've got to be more Carlo. But then if you're a bit more relaxed sometimes and people are on the pitch, not doing their job, sometimes you've got a bit more Jose."

Lampard said he is not driven by trying to convince the sceptics after leading Coventry back to the Premier League for the first time in 25 years.

"The thing about modern-day football – you're brilliant one minute, you might not be brilliant the next and then everyone will let you know that," he told musician and Sky Blues fan Tom Grennan.

"You've got to be careful trying to prove every doubter wrong, because it's not possible."

Lampard guided Coventry to win the Championship with 95 points last season after taking over at the club in November 2024.

Prior to that, his managerial experience could be described as a mixed bag. After taking over at Derby in 2018, the former Chelsea midfielder led them to the Championship play-off final, where they lost to Aston Villa.

Following that, he had abortive spells in the Premier League with Chelsea and Everton, lasting 18 months at Stamford Bridge before being sacked in January 2021, and lasting less than a year at Goodison Park before being sacked in January 2023.

"My personal ambition to prove any doubters wrong is sort of always there, but I try not to let that be my driver," Lampard explained.

"I've been in the Premier League as a player, I've been as a manager, I understand the challenge of it. I can't get ahead of myself and I can't worry too much about the outside world because otherwise you succumb to it, you'd be making different decisions."

As a player, Lampard won three Premier League titles and the Champions League in 2012. He also won four FA Cups, two League Cups and the Europa League.

He described last season's promotion with Coventry as being on par with some of those achievements.

"When you get promoted, it's hard to balance against winning the Champions League with Chelsea," Lampard said.

"Winning in Munich was the best footballing night of my life as a player by far. But then when you do something with a club that's been through what it's been through, when you work with a group of lads that are so great as a dressing room - I've never experienced, especially as a coach, to have such a good group.

"When we got promoted against Blackburn, I had a rush of pure emotion, it all came on top of me. It certainly goes right up there in things I've managed to achieve."

Lampard said that his side will have to adapt to the different challenge this season after entering the top flight, especially defensively.

"We want to keep hold of the good things from last year," he added.

"We'd be fools to think that we'd just go and play like we did in the 'Champ' every week when we dominated a lot of games."

In terms of ambitions for the season, he wants his players to be brave.

"Everyone's going to ask me, 'staying in the league, is that your target?'," Lampard said.

"Of course it would be success, because it's such a big challenge for us, but in the beginning, we'll go into it and go, 'let's stick our chests out and let's be brave about it'.

"These boys have earned where they've got to, so go in with that attitude. There's a lot to lose, but go and show yourselves."

Coventry lost 3-0 to champions Arsenal in the opening match of the season. They will host fellow promoted side Hull City on Saturday, in their first home game of the campaign.

title: Labour rejects Zack Polanski’s call to ‘slam brakes’ on building AI datacentres
description:
Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy
Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”.
The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
Government says Green leader’s proposed moratorium on ‘energy-guzzling’ AI projects would be disaster for economy

Labour has rejected calls to pause construction of major AI infrastructure in Britain after the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, said it was time to “slam the brakes on these energy-guzzling, water-guzzling datacentres”.

The government hit back at the opposition party’s proposal of a “moratorium other than [for] local-scale datacentres for the local community”, saying it “would be a disaster for jobs and national security”.

The Greens’ call for a pause comes amid one of the UK’s worst droughts in years and predictions that datacentres’ electricity use, now standing at about 2.5% of the UK’s supply, will rise fourfold by 2030.

Datacentres contain the processing chips that power billions of AI prompts every day and Labour has designated them as critical national infrastructure, a decision Polanski called “outrageous”. “To most people critical infrastructure means hospitals, water, electricity,” he said. “It doesn’t mean artificial intelligence.”

He added: “Right now the government is putting our communities, our water security and our climate ambitions second to the demands of tech giants.”

A spokesperson for the government said: “A pause on building new datacentres would simply send investment and good jobs abroad, while leaving Britain dependent on overseas computing for the processing of sensitive health and defence data.”

They said critical national infrastructure status did not give datacentres priority access to water or electricity, nor did it automatically put them ahead of households during shortages, and that in England datacentres’ water usage represented less than 1% of non-household water consumption.

The row comes amid increasing signs that datacentre policy, already a major political issue in the US midterm elections, is rising up the agenda in Britain. In energy- and water-rich Scotland, the Scottish National party government appears to be “inching towards a moratorium” amid voter pressure, while local disputes have erupted from Devon to Buckinghamshire and Cardiff to Fife where residents have raised fears about noise, heat, traffic and the visual impact of datacentres affecting house prices.

The AI minister, Kanishka Narayan, has linked the need for more AI datacentres to strong defence and this month claimed the British public “doesn’t just want foreign billionaires to own things that matter to our lives. If we’re being true to those British values, it is impossible to achieve that without building a sovereign level of datacentre capacity.”

The government spokesperson said its refusal to pause development “does not mean a blank cheque for big tech or that every datacentre should be approved”. They said developers should “prioritise clean power, use water responsibly, create British jobs and supply chains, and provide investment to the communities in which they are built”.

The tech equity campaign group Foxglove warned that with some datacentre developers seeking to mitigate long waits to connect to the energy grid by planning their own gas-fired power stations, there was a risk of a “deeply alarming backward step on climate action”.

Rosa Curling, its co-executive director, said: “It’s good to hear that the government thinks there shouldn’t be a ‘blank cheque’ for big tech’s datacentres. But without urgent action, that’s exactly what will happen – the public and the planet will be left to foot the bill for the environmental and social costs of these energy-hungry giants.”

title: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stopped
description: Her family is among hundreds anxiously waiting for news after the deadly flash floods.
fullText:
Early on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.

She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.

Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.

Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.

The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years.

Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.

But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message.

"After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.

Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.

The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement.

In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square.

She told her husband the countryside was beautiful.

"She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."

The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.

She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night.

She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.

Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one.

A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.

There was little to suggest what was coming.

"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."

The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.

Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.

After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.

Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck.

"I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."

At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.

He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.

The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since.

"Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."

He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards.

"Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."

Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."

For the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.

They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.

Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.

Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu.

"She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."

Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family.

"She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."

She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said.

The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina outside the Nepal immigration centre.

Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.

"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says. "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."

For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.

Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains.

Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.

Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list of 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.

For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

title: Autopsy shows Tennessee National Guard fatally shot 20-year-old armed man in the back
description: Tennessee National Guard members assigned to a federal anti-crime task force in Memphis fatally shot an armed 20-year-old man in the back in July, an autopsy report obtained by The Associated Press sh...
fullText:
Tennessee National Guard members assigned to a federal anti-crime task force in Memphis fatally shot an armed 20-year-old man in the back in July, an autopsy report obtained by The Associated Press shows, contradicting police accounts that the man was facing the troops when they fired.

Authorities have said Tyrin Johnson turned toward guard members with a gun while running from them in the early morning hours after the Fourth of July holiday when he was fatally shot in the chest.

But according to an autopsy report shared Thursday by Johnson's family, a single bullet went in the right side of his back and exited through his upper right chest. The autopsy findings, reported earlier by The Commercial Appeal newspaper, were prepared by the West Tennessee Regional Forensic Center Office of the Medical Examiner, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The guard members were assigned to the Memphis Safe Task Force, created by President Donald Trump, who last year sent troops and federal agents to Democratic-run cities that he described as overrun with crime. The task force was involved in four fatal shootings between May and July.

Johnson's grandfather, Evaniel Johnson, said guard members had no justification to shoot his grandson in the back.

"If he ain't caused you no threat, you know what I'm saying, you have no reason to be killing," said the former correctional officer with the Davidson County Sheriff's Office in Nashville.

Officers responded to a call of shots fired a few blocks from Beale Street and saw a person armed with a gun leaving, said Memphis police. Two Guard members responded to the Memphis police radio call, left their vehicle and approached the suspect, who "rounded on them and pointed a tan handgun at them," according to a Tennessee National Guard report obtained by the Associated Press. Both troops fired their service weapons, M17 handguns, and Memphis police arrived shortly after, the guard report said.

The bullet had a slightly upward trajectory through Tyrin Johnson's body, the autopsy report said. That would be consistent with him running away from the shooter, said Dr. Steven White, a certified forensic pathologist who did not do Johnson's autopsy but reviewed the report for the AP.

The report said there was no soot, gunpowder stippling or muzzle imprint around the wound, which White said indicated Johnson was likely shot from more than 3 feet away.

"Be transparent – you shot him in the back," Evaniel Johnson added. "I just want to make sure somebody be responsible for what happened. Some accountability. They ain't never going to bring my grandson back."

In the autopsy report, an "investigative narrative" based on an account from an agent with the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation also stated Tyrin Johnson was turning toward law enforcement with a gun.

"The unknown male grabbed at his waistband," the report stated. "Law enforcement officers saw the unknown male draw a firearm. Law enforcement officers then shot at the unknown male, striking him once in the chest."

Andre Wharton, an attorney representing Johnson's family, told the AP that the narrative presented by law enforcement does not match the autopsy findings of a single bullet wound in the back.

"I just see some kind of blatant inconsistency there, in terms of what law enforcement reports," Wharton said. "The versions don't seem to match."

The manner of death is listed as "homicide," which typically is used when a death is caused by the actions of another person but often doesn't factor in intent or carry any legal weight. To date, no criminal charges have been filed.

TBI said the investigation is "open and ongoing" and directed AP to the medical examiner's office when asked to confirm the autopsy findings. The AP has a pending request for a copy for Johnson's autopsy from the Shelby County Medical Examiner's office.

Johnson was carrying a "handgun magazine with rounds," according to the autopsy report. Wharton said it was not illegal for Johnson to be carrying the ammunition in Tennessee.

Johnson's family has asked authorities to show them surveillance video or other evidence he was pointing a weapon at guard members. The family has still not been shown any video of the moments leading up to the shooting, Evaniel Johnson said.

Trump's decision to send Tennessee National Guard troops to Memphis to combat crime was met with a mixed response from residents and was the subject of a lawsuit, though it did not result in widespread protests.

title: Trump has his eye on these Pacific island nations
description: Trump's latest Truth Social post labels two Pacific island nations as U.S. territories, fueling fresh questions about his expansion ambitions.
fullText:
A new Truth Social post from President Donald Trump is raising eyebrows after it appeared to portray two Pacific island nations as U.S. territories, even though both are independent countries.

The post adds Micronesia and the Marshall Islands to a growing list of places Trump has discussed bringing under U.S. ownership, control or influence.

The White House has not explained the post, but it is the latest example of Trump's interest in expanding U.S. influence beyond its current borders. Since returning to office, the president has revived calls to acquire Greenland, floated the idea of making Venezuela the 51st state and suggested the United States could one day claim control of the Strait of Hormuz.

USA TODAY contacted the White House for comment but had not received a response as of Aug. 28.

More: 'Lake America'? Trump's Canada snub prompts backlash – from Americans

The Marshall Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia may be independent countries, but both have deep historical ties to the United States.

After World War II, the United States administered both island nations as part of a U.N.-backed trust territory in the Pacific. The Marshall Islands gained independence in 1979, while Micronesia became independent in 1990.

Even after independence, the countries maintained close ties with Washington through what's known as a Compact of Free Association, or COFA.

Under the agreements, the United States provides financial assistance and access to certain federal services, while retaining key defense and security responsibilities in the region.

According to the Department of the Interior, the compacts give residents of the Marshall Islands and Micronesia access to programs and services that include the U.S. Postal Service and National Weather Service. The agreements have also made the islands important U.S. partners in a strategically significant part of the Pacific.

Those longstanding ties help explain why the two nations are often closely associated with the United States, even though they are sovereign countries rather than U.S. territories.

The Marshall Islands and Micronesia are not the first places to become wrapped up in Trump's comments about expanding U.S. territory.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has repeatedly argued that Greenland, the autonomous Danish territory in the Arctic, is critical to U.S. national security. The president first floated the idea of purchasing Greenland during his first term before reviving the proposal after his reelection.

"We need Greenland for national security," Trump said in December. "You look up and down the coast, you have Russian and Chinese ships all over the place. We need it for national security. We have to have it."

Trump has also turned his attention to Venezuela. Earlier this year, he said he had seriously considered making the oil-rich South American nation the 51st U.S. state. The idea gained renewed attention following a U.S. military operation that led to the arrest of former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores.

The president has since suggested the United States could temporarily oversee Venezuela and its oil infrastructure, adding the country to a growing list of territories and strategic locations Trump has discussed bringing under greater U.S. control.

With Micronesia and the Marshall Islands now appearing in a post labeled "U.S. Territories," Trump's latest social media message is fueling fresh questions about how far those ambitions extend.

USA TODAY's Joey Garrison and Reuters contributed to this report.

Fernando Cervantes Jr. is a trending news reporter for USA TODAY. Reach him at fernando.cervantes@usatodayco.com and follow him on X @fern_cerv_.

title: Judge again blocks Trump mail ballot executive order in ruling that’s likely to be swiftly appealed
description: A federal judge on Thursday halted — at least for now — attempts to implement President Donald Trump’s executive order limiting mail voting.  The move stalled the directive for a second time only abou...
fullText:
A federal judge on Thursday halted — at least for now — attempts to implement President Donald Trump's executive order limiting mail voting.

The move stalled the directive for a second time only about a week before the first mail ballots are due to be sent out for the rapidly approaching midterm elections. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani blocked the government from implementing the order for two weeks.

The case could soon be appealed back to the Supreme Court, days after the justices handed down a procedural decision that allowed the the administration to move ahead.

The ruling Thursday came after Democrats and voting rights groups refiled their lawsuits to comply with the recent Supreme Court decision. The high court's conservative majority did not rule on the legality of Trump's executive order, instead saying Talwani had acted too soon.

Now the administration has issued a formal rule governing whether the U.S. Postal Service will deliver states' mail ballots, effectively restarting the legal fight.

The whipsawing legal battle has major ramifications for the midterms. Nearly one-third of Americans vote by mail and election officials contend there isn't enough time to revise their systems to comply with the new Postal Service directives.

The Postal Service says it won't deliver mail ballots unless states provide a list of voters who should receive them and format the envelopes in a certain way.

"Plaintiff states have neither time nor funds to design new mail ballots, seek approval of the new designs, order production of mail ballots, update their own election management systems, train election officials to use the USPS portal and upload citizen data to the portal, all before the midterms," Talwani wrote Thursday.

The White House did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment. A hearing in the case is set for Sept. 3.

"This rule is a clear attempt by the federal government to interfere in elections it has no power to control. Today, a federal court halted it before this administration could wreak havoc on our elections," New York Attorney General Letitia James, one of two dozen Democratic attorneys general who filed one of the suits, said in a statement after the order.

Democrats and voting rights groups contend the Postal Services' demand is unconstitutional. The Constitution, they note, grants states and, in some cases, Congress the power to make election rules — not the president or Postal Service.

That reasoning led courts to block Trump's first executive order, issued last year, that sought to change election procedures, such as requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register.

The president has long targeted mail voting, which he falsely blames for his 2020 election loss even though he himself uses it to cast his ballot.

A report by the Brookings Institution published in 2025 found that mail voting fraud occurred in only about four cases out of every 10 million mail ballots cast.

Trump issued the executive order targeting mail voting, his second one related to elections since he returned from office, in March.

Opponents quickly sued, but the administration argued the claims were premature because it hadn't issued rules outlining how it would implement the order. The administration won an initial case in Washington, D.C., with that reasoning, but Talwani placed injunctions against implementing the order for the November midterms in two separate cases she heard in Boston.

The Supreme Court's conservative majority on Monday struck down one of those holds.

Talwani, nominated to the bench by President Barack Obama, reluctantly removed the second injunction shortly after. The plaintiffs then moved to refile their cases, citing the Postal Service's publishing of its final rule, in hopes of winning a more durable victory.

title: I dropped out of college to sell Pokémon cards full time. My business made $7.8 million in sales last year alone.
description: Andres Fernandez dropped out of his business degree in college and built a Pokémon cards had $7.8 million in sales in 2025, mainly from Whatnot.
fullText:
Andres Fernandez dropped out of his business degree program in college to found his own company.

The company, MintlyCollects, made $7.8 million in sales in 2025 and became a family business.

Fernandez said that he believes you can't "just go with the flow" and find a direction in life.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Andres Fernandez, founder and CEO of MintlyCollects, which specializes in selling Pokémon cards on the live selling platform, Whatnot. The company's two Whatnot accounts have around 500k followers altogether. The essay has been edited for length and clarity.

I was born and raised in Miami, and I've always been an out-of-the-box kid.

When I signed up for college, I didn't really know what I wanted to do. I was going to college because my mom was making me go, and I was studying business, which I find to be cliché.

After just one semester, I dropped out to be a full-time Pokémon card seller.

Rather than getting a business degree to work a corporate job, I ended up building a real business that's mine.

I was super into video games, YouTube, Twitch, and content creation growing up. I had played Pokémon video games since I was 10, but I wasn't a collector. That changed when my little cousin's birthday came around, and I needed to get him a gift.

I went to Target and bought him some cards. We opened the cards together at his birthday party, and he pulled a $100 card from a $5 pack. As soon as I saw that, I was like, "I'm in. This is awesome."

I started collecting and ripping a lot of packs. At the time, I was working at a croqueta bar, frying food for $10 an hour. I was spending too much money on Pokémon cards, so I started creating content around Pokémon.

I eventually grew an account to about 30,000 followers and started selling on Instagram Live. Then Whatnot reached out to me.

I joined in late 2020, when Whatnot had just started its Pokémon side. I was probably one of the first five Pokémon streamers on the platform.

I saw the vision immediately. I grew up watching YouTube and Twitch, so I thought, "Imagine being on YouTube when YouTube first started." If you're consistent, you're going to succeed because as the platform succeeds, you're going to grow with it.

For the first two to three years, I did everything myself. I streamed six days a week, packed orders, shipped them, and repeated the process Monday through Saturday.

My uncle eventually sat me down and said, "You're onto something. Quit your job. Stop school, and run with it."

title: Haiti receives nearly 200,000 forced deportees, UN says after brutal gang killing
description: Nearly 200,000 people were forcibly returned to Haiti in the first eight months of this year, a U.N. official told an emergency meeting of the Security Council on
fullText:
Aug 28 (Reuters) - Nearly 200,000 people were forcibly returned to Haiti in the first eight months of this year, a U.N. official told an emergency meeting of the Security Council on Friday, days after ‌a brutal gang attack killed nearly 50 people near the capital.

The forced return represents at least 20,000 more ‌people than in the same period last year, Indrika Ratwatte, the acting assistant secretary-general for humanitarian affairs, told the meeting.

Sunday night's attack took place days after ​Haiti received its first U.S. deportation flight since the Trump administration won a legal battle ending Temporary Protected Status for around 350,000 Haitians. On Thursday, another flight arrived with migrants from the U.S. and the Bahamas.

Haitian security analysts have meanwhile warned that the flood of illegal arms entering the country is worsening the conflict that has claimed more than 21,000 lives since 2022.

The U.N. estimates most guns ‌in Haiti originate from the southeastern United States, ⁠though many are trafficked into the country through the land border with the Dominican Republic.

Ratwatte briefed the Security Council alongside Carlos Ruiz, the head of the U.N. Integrated Office in Haiti (BINUH), who warned ⁠that without improved security, efforts to advance preparations for the country's first elections in a decade remain "severely constrained and vulnerable to setbacks."

Ruiz said three boys and two girls were among the 47 people killed in the hillside community of Kenscoff near the capital Port-au-Prince on Sunday, ​where houses ​were set on fire and people who sought to escape were ​attacked inside a church.

"This latest heartbreaking episode is a ‌stark reminder of the urgent need to further strengthen international security support for Haiti," Ruiz said.

U.N.-BACKED FORCE'S MANDATE NEARS END

Diplomats argued the attack showed the need to more rapidly scale up the deployment of the U.N.-backed multinational force mandated to help police fight gangs that have massively expanded their influence over the last five years.

Haitian authorities first requested foreign military assistance in 2022, but this was slow to materialize, and a year ago the U.N. mandated a different, larger and more aggressive force to deploy, ‌called the Gang Suppression Force (GSF).

The GSF aims to reach a capacity of ​5,500 troops by fall this year. The Security Council will vote on whether ​to renew its mandate at the end of September.

U.S. ​representative Jennifer Locetta called on the Security Council to renew the mandate.

"The GSF was not created to ‌issue statements from within a compound wall or spend ​our money while Haiti suffers," ​she said, adding if more countries bring material support to the force, it could help police fight gangs more efficiently.

"This attack is precisely why the U.N. authorized Gang Suppression Force's mission and mandate matters," she said.

A representative for the ​Haitian government said Chad, Mongolia and Ivory ‌Coast had agreed to support the force and work was under way for similar agreements with Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, ​Jamaica and Guatemala. The latter two countries had already deployed personnel under a prior iteration of the ​force.

title: Lawsuit alleges Freedom Fuel gas stations touted by Trump are selling stolen fuel
description: The stations around Philadelphia and New Jersey had raised questions about how they were able to undercut rival retailers.
fullText:
A lawsuit filed this month alleges that there's a simple reason some stations in the Freedom Fuel Network — the chain of discount gas stations promoted by the White House — have been able to sell gas so cheaply: Some $4 million worth of the gas is stolen.

KRSM, the business named in the suit, denies this accusation.

Freedom Fuel stations located around Philadelphia and New Jersey burst into public view in the run-up to the July Fourth holiday, when President Donald Trump posted praise for their discounted pump prices, writing "They are doing this because they love the U.S.A." The White House later posted a video of drivers filling up at one of the stations and thanking Trump for the low prices — at the time, $3.47 a gallon in honor of the 47th president, though they've since crept up.

Neither the White House nor the network's owners would explain exactly how the stations were able to sell fuel far cheaper than their competitors. The White House told reporters that Freedom Fuel was simply a private company lowering its margins for patriotic reasons and declined to disclose the people behind it — who turned out to be a former New Jersey mayor and NFL special teams coach for the Baltimore Ravens, a GOP donor.

POLITICO's reporting also linked six of the stations via business records to a New Jersey fuel businessperson named Shamikh Kazmi who, along with his brother Syed Kazmi, have been involved in several lawsuits. The Freedom Fuel Network's website said that despite "misinformation and baseless speculation … Freedom Fuel Network is proudly lowering prices to benefit our community and strengthen our local economy."

But according to a complaint filed Aug. 19 by Georgia-based fuel supplier Mansfield Oil Co. in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, Syed Kazmi's company KRSM acquired over 1 million gallons of fuel from a Sunoco terminal in Twin Oaks valued at around $4 million — and never paid for it. KRSM sold some of the fuel, the lawsuit alleges, to stations within the Freedom Fuel Network, which now claims to operate 29 locations.

"KRSM was able to sell such fuel for such low prices and garner such publicity because it never paid Plaintiffs for such fuel," reads the complaint.

KRSM disputed the allegations in an emailed statement, calling the case "an accounting dispute over fuel invoices misplaced by Mansfield Oil" and continuing: "We will not be commenting further on this pending litigation." A message to Freedom Fuel sent via its website was not returned. Shamikh Kazmi did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

"Syed Kazmi is a principal owner, and President, of KRSM, Inc," said Urs Broderick Furrer, a lawyer for Mansfield, in a statement. "KRSM has failed to pay for fuel that they lifted off of Mansfield's account. That is not an accounting dispute. The fuel was delivered to at least 10 of the Freedom Fuel Network locations, as listed on the Freedom Fuel Network's website."

A White House official said that "the Administration has had zero contact or dealings with the defendant: KRSM Inc or Sayed Kazmi." And a source familiar with the Freedom Fuel business said that "KRSM Inc and Sayed Kazmi are not associated with the Freedom Fuel Network in any capacity."

Companies associated with the Kazmis have previously been subject to other lawsuits alleging fraudulent activity and theft. For instance, a federal judge entered judgment in February in favor of a fuel distributor that alleged in a civil lawsuit that Shamikh Kazmi's company had taken roughly $667,000 worth of fuel over 10 days in August 2021 without fully paying for it. Shamikh Kazmi denied the allegations, but the court entered a default judgment after what the judge described as the defendants and their lawyers' "serial flouting of Court orders and the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure" during the case.

In another suit, 7-Eleven accused Syed Kazmi's KRSM in 2022 of stealing tens of thousands of dollars worth of cigarettes, and the judge again found in favor of the plaintiff in 2024. KRSM disputed 7-Eleven's allegations of breach of contract, claiming 7-Eleven was the one that breached the contract.

The current lawsuit also alleges that KRSM is not authorized to conduct business in Pennsylvania or New Jersey at all. New Jersey's Division of Consumer Affairs declined to comment. The Pennsylvania attorney general's office did not respond to a request for comment.

James Bikales contributed to this report.

title: Hochul boasts 'I just banned it' as New York outlaws local police partnerships with ICE
description: Kathy Hochul says 287(g) agreements are now banned in New York, but DHS warns the restriction will force more federal agents into communities.
fullText:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday on "Morning Joe" that New York banned formal civil immigration enforcement agreements between local law enforcement and ICE because she wants officers focused on local crime.

A DHS spokesperson said in an exclusive statement to Fox News Digital that the restriction will force more federal agents into communities as 15 county sheriffs challenge the law in federal court.

"When politicians bar local law enforcement from working with DHS, our law enforcement officers have to have a more visible presence so that we can find and apprehend the criminals let out of jails and back into communities," the DHS spokesperson said.

Border Czar Homan Vows To 'Flood' New York With Ice Agents Despite Hochul's Resistance

"Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE. Instead of working with us, Governor Hochul and Attorney General James are choosing to RELEASE violent criminals from their jails directly back into our communities to perpetrate more crimes and create more victims."

DHS cited five New York cases involving noncitizens who it said remained at large or were released despite ICE detainers after arrests or convictions involving attempted murder, rape, assault, weapons charges or child endangerment. ICE later took all five into custody, and one was removed to Mexico, the department said.

Hochul's office responded to DHS's criticism Friday in a statement to Fox News Digital, disputing the department's characterization of the law's public safety consequences.

"Governor Hochul has been clear: You don't make New York State safer by co-opting local law enforcement to conduct civil immigration enforcement that targets families, children and hardworking individuals," a Hochul spokesperson said.

"A federal court has already upheld New York's Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, and the state will continue to work with federal and local law enforcement in cracking down on violent offenders while keeping our communities safe and enforcing our laws."

During the interview on "Morning Joe," co-host Willie Geist asked whether ICE could still secure agreements with New York police forces.

Dem Governor In The Hot Seat After Testing Limits Of Authority With Major Move Against Ice

"I just banned it," Hochul said. "It's against the law now in the state of New York to have these agreements."

The Local Cops, Local Crimes Act, signed in May, took effect Tuesday. It prohibits state and local entities from entering or remaining in 287(g) agreements, which allow trained local personnel to perform certain federal civil immigration functions under ICE supervision.

Hochul's office said the law does not prevent jails from notifying ICE about potentially deportable people in custody or transferring someone lawfully in custody to the agency, subject to local laws.

Existing corrections law also requires the state Department of Corrections and Community Supervision to notify federal immigration authorities after receiving a noncitizen into custody, the governor's office said.

New York Sheriffs 'Mad As Hell' As Hochul Pushes To Ban Key Law Enforcement Partnership

The federal lawsuit, led by Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault, claims the ban unlawfully overrides independently elected sheriffs' authority and impairs federally authorized agreements. The state said Rensselaer was the only one of 12 agencies with a 287(g) agreement that had not indicated it would dissolve the pact.

Attorney General Letitia James sued Rensselaer County and its sheriff Thursday, seeking an order terminating the agreement. The action was the first filed by the state's new Office of Immigrant Trust.

A federal judge earlier this month denied the Justice Department's request for a preliminary injunction against the 287(g) ban in a separate case, allowing Tuesday's deadline to take effect. That litigation remains pending, and the 15 sheriffs have separately requested emergency relief in their new case.

Original article

title: A Dutch institute issues a 'Red Alert' over potentially lethal Trump-shaped ecstasy pills
description: A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute warned users on Friday about potentially lethal ecstasy pills shaped to look like the head of U.S. President Donald Trump.  The respected Trimbos Ins...
fullText:
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — A Dutch drug addiction and mental health institute warned users on Friday about potentially lethal ecstasy pills shaped to look like the head of U.S. President Donald Trump.

The respected Trimbos Institute said that several of the pills have been handed in recently at a network of centers that test drugs for users before they take them.

"Absolutely do not use these pills," the institute warned.

It released a photo of the pills that have a depiction of Trump's head on one side and on the other side "NL" and "Trump" stamped into the surface either side of a vertical line. One of the pills has a green face and another is yellow.

The institute warned in a " Red Alert " published on its website and social media that they contain a high concentration of a chemical called PMMA, or para-methoxymethamfetamine, that is similar to MDMA, the active ingredient in ecstasy pills.

However, PMMA is slower working than MDMA and that could lead users to take more because they think that the first pill didn't work, leading to a risk of overdosing, the institute said, adding that use of the pills "can lead to overheating with possibly deadly consequences."

Spokesperson Anniek Groothuis said that the institute has no reported cases of serious illness or fatalities among people who may have used the drug.

"We do not know of any victims where PMMA was found in their blood," she told The Associated Press.

Producing, selling and using ecstasy is illegal in the Netherlands, but it's widely used, particularly at clubs and music festivals. A government report in 2024 said that some 550,000 people took the drug in a year.

It's not the first time ecstasy pills in the form of Trump's head have appeared. In 2017, German police seized thousands of orange Trump-shaped tablets.

title: I spent my Saturday with the Target exec on a mission to fix its stores
description: Back to school season is second only to the holidays in terms of importance for Target. We went behind the scenes to see how it's going.
fullText:
Back-to-school is Target's biggest shopping moment outside of the holidays.

Business Insider went behind the scenes with Target's stores chief to see how it's tackling the rush.

"This is the 16th state in three weeks of visits," Adrienne Costanzo told us.

If the holiday shopping season is a retailer's final exam each year, back-to-school is the midterms. For Target, this year's test is a big one.

Success depends on getting the basics right: exciting merchandise, fully stocked stores, and competitive pricing. Those are all areas where Target has stumbled in recent years.

This year's season is also an early read on CEO Michael Fiddelke's turnaround plan. He took the reins earlier this year after a rough patch for Target, which faced boycotts in 2025 after winding down several diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Last week, it faced fresh criticism over a children's Halloween costume resembling racist minstrel imagery; Target pulled it and apologized.

To see how Target is trying to pull it off, Business Insider visited a pair of stores in Madison, Wisconsin, with chief stores officer Adrienne Costanzo.

Costanzo is a 22-year veteran of Target and has held numerous roles in HR and store operations. Her appointment to her current position came in February 2025, roughly six months before Fiddelke was announced as CEO. She's now responsible for more than 350,000 workers across 2,000 stores in all 50 US states.

This month, Costanzo has logged serious miles to check in with shoppers, employees, and store managers about what's working and what isn't in their stores as they head back to school.

"This is the 16th state in three weeks of visits," she said while in Madison. "I've been to Michigan, I've been to Nebraska, I mean, I've been like everywhere."

On the Saturday of this visit, grade-school parents were gearing up for the first day of class, and college students at the University of Wisconsin were kitting out their apartments. Dorm move-ins were still a week away, and both locations were doing brisk business.

Unlike the holidays, different school seasons peak at different times, creating all manner of complexity for inventory planning and staffing, Fiddelke told investors on a second-quarter earnings call.

"The foot traffic is incredible — the parents and students," Costanzo said of her multi-state tour.

Her visits include conversations with shoppers who express relief at Target's improved in-stock rates and positive impressions of collaborations with brands like LoveShackFancy and Hollister, she said. It's a return to the sort of merchandising that helps draw customers into stores and tempts them to add unexpected finds to an already full shopping cart.

Cale Makar contract makes him NHL's first $20M man: Why deal is worth it for Avalanche
description: Cale Makar's contract makes him the NHL's highest-paid player. He's well worth the payout.
fullText:
Colorado Avalanche star defenseman Cale Makar could be one of the last NHL players to sign an eight-year contract, and he and the team made it a record-breaker.

He'll make $163.2 million in the extension he signed on Friday, Aug. 28 and have a record $20.4 million average annual value. He's the NHL's first $20 million player.

After Sept. 15, the maximum contract length goes to seven years for a player re-signing with his team and six years for a player signing with another team.

But this extension means Makar is under contract for nine more seasons with the Avalanche. Here's a look at the deal and how it affects the team's competitive window:

Yes, especially considering how much salaries have risen recently. He's a two-time winner of the Norris Trophy and has been a top-three finalist in the six years since he won rookie of the year.

He was the fourth-fastest defenseman to reach 500 points, trailing only Hall of Famers Bobby Orr, Paul Coffey and Denis Potvin. He's averaging more than a point per game in the regular season (Orr and Coffey were the only defensemen to finish their careers that way) and has 90 points in 90 playoff games.

Makar was playoff MVP when the Avalanche won the Stanley Cup in 2022. As a sign of his importance, the No. 1 overall Avalanche were swept in the 2026 Western Conference finals with injured Makar unable to play the first two games.

Having Makar around for nine seasons will help. He and Devon Toews are the NHL's best defensive tandem, and Makar is signed through 2034-35 and Toews through 2030-31.

Top offensive forwards Nathan MacKinnon and Martin Necas are also signed through 2031.

Makar's cap hit falls just short of the maximum 20%, but don't forget that the cap is going up. It's jumping to $113.5 million next season and Makar's annual average value is only 18% of that. There will be room to build around the core.

Makar is 27 and should remain productive well into the deal. He has been durable with only one season dealing with significant injuries.

His deal will keep the Avalanche competitive now and well into the future.

title: Dan Campbell Delivers Powerful Message to High School Football Players
description: Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell delivered a passionate message to high school football players as the 2026 season begins, reminding seniors and underclassmen alike how quickly the experience disappears.
fullText:
Dan Campbell has spent most of his adult life around football.

He played 11 seasons in the NFL, reached a Super Bowl, moved into coaching and eventually became the head coach of the Detroit Lions.

Yet when Campbell was asked Thursday about high school football, his mind did not immediately drift toward the NFL.

Freshly cut grass. Friday nights. Teammates you have known since you were kids. Practices that feel endless at the time and impossibly short years later.

With high school football returning across Michigan this week, Campbell delivered a message that had very little to do with wins, statistics or college recruiting.

The timing could not have been much better.

The 2026 Michigan high school football season opened this week, with the MHSAA estimating that roughly 33,000 players are participating across the state. The opening schedule included 184 games Thursday, another 112 Friday and six Saturday.

For thousands of seniors, every one of those games now comes with a shrinking number attached.

Campbell understands that better now than he did when he was wearing the uniform.

"Make the most of it," Campbell said. "Because you're not guaranteed to be able to get another chance to play and be with those guys that you grew up with and enjoy the game at that level and the wins and the sacrifice and the hard work and the blood and the sweat and the tears. It's a special time, enjoy it."

It is a different version of Campbell than Lions fans typically see.

This is the same coach who has built Detroit around competition, physicality and accountability. Those principles have been evident again throughout a summer in which Campbell believed Detroit benefited from spending training camp competing against itself.

But Campbell's message to high school players was not about toughness for toughness's sake.

It was about understanding what the game gives you before that version of the game disappears.

Campbell grew up in Texas and played at Glen Rose High School before eventually continuing his career at Texas A&M.

The New York Giants selected Campbell in the third round of the 1999 NFL Draft. He eventually played for the Giants, Dallas Cowboys and Lions before beginning a coaching career that has now lasted well over a decade.

There have been NFL playoff games. Packed stadiums. A Super Bowl appearance as a player. Another run to the NFC Championship Game as Detroit's coach.

Yet Campbell still remembers how his high school career ended.

"We lost, and it wasn't good. Yeah, we weren't going to the playoffs, I remember that," Campbell said. "But I remember being with that group of guys that I knew and I grew up with and I was with for a long time. And it is, you don't forget those, you just don't. You just don't forget and it is a special time. And you're going to look back and wish, 'Man, I wish I could do that one more time. I wish I could go back and play that game one more time or play with those guys one more time.'"

That is probably the part of Campbell's message that resonates most.

Very few high school football players will eventually play in the NFL.

Many will never play another organized football game after high school.

But that does not make what they are doing now less important.

In some ways, that is exactly what makes it important.

The locker rooms change. Teammates scatter. Friday night becomes something you drive past instead of something you spend an entire week preparing for.

Campbell has reached levels of football most players can only imagine, and he still remembers the guys standing beside him before any of that happened.

Campbell did not limit his advice to seniors.

He also challenged freshmen and sophomores to understand what this season means to the older players in their locker room.

"If you're a young guy, man, I'm a freshman, I'm a sophomore, you owe it to the seniors because this may be the last time that, you get one more shot, they don't," Campbell said. "So, give them everything you have got and make it a special year for them because next year is your year and you're going to want those young guys to help you. So, man, enjoy it. It doesn't last and you'll remember it the rest of your life."

There is plenty of Campbell's coaching philosophy buried in that answer.

Accountability is not merely doing your job because a coach told you to do it.

It is understanding that somebody else is counting on you.

Campbell has spent years trying to establish that mentality with the Lions, whether he is challenging a young player during training camp or demanding more from Detroit after a sloppy preseason performance.

In high school, the stakes are obviously different.

Your season is also somebody else's final season.

Your rep affects somebody else's memory.

Your effort becomes part of somebody else's last Friday night.

There is a reason Campbell's words work without sounding like a motivational poster taped to a locker room wall.

Campbell knows what football can become because it became his profession.

He also knows what it once was.

Before the NFL contracts, before coaching staffs, before Ford Field and before tens of thousands of people were analyzing every decision he made, football meant lining up next to people he grew up with.

Most high school players will eventually walk away from the sport.

They will remember some scores. They will remember a touchdown, a big hit or a rivalry win.

But years later, the details that stick may be different.

The jokes nobody outside the team understood.

The teammate who lined up next to you.

Campbell has been around football long enough to know how quickly all of it disappears.

And while you still have the chance, enjoy the hell out of it.

title: Packers rookie Dani Dennis-Sutton gets QB sack in preseason debut
description: It didn't take Packers rookie edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton long to make an impact in his preseason debut.
fullText:
It did not take long for Green Bay Packers rookie edge rusher Dani Dennis-Sutton to make an impact play in his preseason debut on Friday night. On the opening drive for the Arizona Cardinals, Dennis-Sutton won on an explosive inside move and sacked veteran quarterback Gardner Minshew for a 10-yard loss to help stall a scoring drive.

The rookie rusher got inside on a stunt, beating both the right tackle and right guard before taking down Minshew in the backfield. The sack came on 2nd-and-10, pushed the Cardinals into a 3rd-and-20 situation and eventually forced a field goal attempt.

DANI DENIED

📺: Packers TV Network pic.twitter.com/Xhv8pGYxdA

While the sack won't count for the rookie's career stats, it did provide an exciting moment for a player who is expected to help the Packers in the pass-rushing department.

Dennis-Sutton, a fourth-round pick of the Packers, is making his preseason debut after missing the first two games with a heat-related illness.

With Micah Parsons expected to start the season on the PUP list, the Packers are likely to keep Dennis-Sutton, Lukas Van Ness, Barryn Sorrell, Brenton Cox and Collin Oliver at edge rusher.

title: ‘Transphobes are pathetic’: Transgender golfer not apologizing to ‘deeply unwell’ bigots after run of dominance
description: The role of transgender athletes participating in women’s sports has become one of the biggest debates in the country following Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham’s comments on the matter in an ESPN profile earlier this summer. “I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I’m like, ‘I never once said that,'”…
fullText:
The role of transgender athletes participating in women's sports has become one of the biggest debates in the country following Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham's comments on the matter in an ESPN profile earlier this summer.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I'm like, 'I never once said that,'" Cunningham said. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Since Cunningham's initial comments, everyone from sports media members to opposing coaches to the White House has weighed in. Now, the debate has reached Alberta, Canada. Transgender golfers Veronica Ivy and Rachel Elser have won five individual women's golf championships this summer, and aren't apologizing for it.

"To the bigots: stay mad, and get a better hobby," Ivy wrote, according to Outkick. "You're deeply unwell and you're obsessed with harassing a stranger. You're not going to make me stop existing and succeeding. I feel really sorry for you. You have my pity."

Alberta Golf updated its official policy to be more inclusive of all competitors in 2025. The organization's rules read as follows:

"For individuals who have undergone gender reassignment after puberty, the following guidelines will be used: I. Male-to-female transgendered persons, to compete as a female, must submit documentation from a medical practitioner that gender reassignment has been ongoing for at least one year."

They just see that I won some competition–without any checking for what level of competition it was," Ivy told OutSports of her detractors earlier this month. "I went from competing in elite world-level track cycling, though never making the national team or the Olympics, to contesting for age group provincial titles.

"I still haven't cracked the top 10 at the Canadian national mid-amateur championship. I'm just out here trying my best, being a good competitor. Transphobes are pathetic."

Hopefully, both Ivy and Elser will keep competing and living their lives to their fullest.

title: Angel Reese records 28th double-double, ties Alyssa Thomas for most in WNBA single-season history
description: Earlier this week, Reese, a 3-time All-Star, set the W's single-game and single-season rebounding records with a 26-board performance.
fullText:
Atlanta Dream forward Angel Reese rebounded from a scoreless first quarter Friday night against the Portland Fire to notch her 28th double-double of the 2026 campaign, tying Phoenix Mercury frontcourt standout Alyssa Thomas for the most in single-season WNBA history.

Through two quarters and change, Reese has put up 10 points and 10 boards in front of her home crowd, four days after she set the W's single-game and single-season rebounding records in Los Angeles with a 26-board performance during a victory over the Sparks.

The 24-year-old three-time All-Star has elevated her game in her first season with the Dream, who acquired the LSU product in a trade with the Chicago Sky this spring. She's averaging north of 16 points per game, and she entered Friday with a league-high 12.4 rebounds per game.

Thomas, a six-time All-Star, logged her 28 double-doubles in 2023 with the Connecticut Sun. Along the way, she piled up double-digit points and assists 11 times. Six of those outings featured triple-doubles (no other WNBA player has more than five triple-doubles all-time, and Thomas has 22 and counting for her career).

All of Reese's double-doubles this season have resulted from her scoring 10-plus points and mounting 10-plus rebounds, the first of which came in her Dream regular-season debut. It's worth noting, however, that she stacked at least five assists in four of her double-doubles. Notably, she sniffed a triple-double last week in a road win over the Sparks that saw her amass 20 points, 10 rebounds and 8 assists. That night, she shot 9 of 9 from the field, including 2 of 2 from beyond the arc, and her Dream rewrote a single-game franchise record with 124 points.

Reese scored a career-high 31 points this past Saturday while helping Atlanta take down Thomas' Mercury on the road. The Dream clinched a playoff berth in the process.

It's been quite the stretch for Reese, the "Bayou Barbie," who's poised for her first postseason after back-to-back years of being on the outside looking in with the Sky.

title: ‘Tiny Hands Tua Tagovailoa,’ ‘Just Needs To Retire’ — NFL Fans Rip Falcons QB’s Major Mistake vs. Dolphins in Preseason
description: One of the remaining quarterback competitions in the NFL is happening with the Atlanta Falcons. While Tua Tagovailoa, the new signing in free agency, had a lead due to health, Michael Penix Jr.
fullText:
One of the remaining quarterback competitions in the NFL is happening with the Atlanta Falcons. While Tua Tagovailoa, the new signing in free agency, had a lead due to health, Michael Penix Jr. is now the favorite. Still, the battle is not done, and Tagovailoa still has a chance to prove himself to the staff.

In the last game of the preseason, the Falcons are facing the Miami Dolphins, which is Tagovailoa's former team. A big chance for the veteran QB, but a significant mistake may have closed the door on Tagovailoa becoming the starter.

With the Dolphins, Tagovailoa had a very up-and-down career, ending with his release from the team. In his last season with the team, Tagovailoa finished 28th in PFN's QB Impact Metric.

There were many things that went into his struggles in Miami, but the Falcons clearly viewed him as a potential starter, especially with Penix Jr. recovering from his ACL injury. Penix Jr. has had a long history of knee issues, so Tagovailoa could have also been a long-term backup plan.

No matter what, preseason was a time for Tagovailoa to prove his worth to the team, but some bad moments from the veteran have put a halt to that possibility. The latest came against the Dolphins, when he fumbled, and Miami recovered.

START PREPARING: PFN's Free Fantasy Draft Simulator

After that play, the NFL World had some major reactions:

A Dolphins fan took a moment to take a shot at Tagovailoa: "Tua doing Tua things."

One fan begged for Tagovailoa to stop fumbling, "Quit fumbling the snaps, Tua!"

Dolphins podcaster Nic Rohloff poked fun at Tagovailoa's hand size and brought up his history of fumbling in games, "Tiny hands Tua will never not fumble the football!"

Another Dolphins fan questioned how Tagovailoa's continues to have his fumbling issues, "LMFAOOOOOO TUA FUMBLE HOW DOES HE FUMBLE SO MUCH???".

BE THE GM OF YOUR FAVORITE TEAM: PFN's Free NFL Mock Draft Simulator

Podcaster Average Joe Sports had some flashbacks to Tagovailoa's time in Miami, and feels like the QB never left, "It's like Tua never left! FUMBLE!"

Another Dolphins fan also jokingly reminisced about Tagovailoa's career with Miami, "Just like old times. Welcome back, Tua #fumble."

One fan mentioned that Tagovailoa should just retire after that fumble, "Turn on Dolphins preseason game just in time to see Tua fumble the ball. He just needs to retire."

Another account, responding to a fan expressing regret about Tagovailoa, brought up the fumble, which reminded them of what the QB would bring to the team: "Tua fumble. That's the guy we remember."

Fantasy football analyst CantaLoupe joked about one of Tagovailoa's fumbles finally helping the Dolphins, "A Tua fumble that actually helps the Dolphins? Now I've seen it all."

Clearly, this was a massive mistake by Tagovailoa, and in a QB battle, it could be what leads the Falcons to choose Penix Jr. instead.

A bit later in the matchup, the Falcons clearly saw enough for Tagovailoa and took him out of the game. He had a decent performance, but it's likely that Penix Jr. will become the Falcons' starter if he gets fully healthy by Week 1.

title: Injury Update: Roster bubble Cowboys LB exits preseason finale

fullText:
The Dallas Cowboys probably didn't have enough room on the roster for third-year pro Marist Liufau. title: San Francisco marathon icon Walt Stack helped to open running for everyone
description: Stack founded the Dolphin South End Runners club in 1966, creating an environment that welcomed women, children and older adults at a time when many running organizations remained exclusive.
fullText:
Long before running became one of America's most popular recreational activities, the sport was largely dominated by men. In the Bay Area, one of the key figures who helped change that was Walt Stack, a runner whose commitment to inclusion influenced generations of athletes.

Stack founded the Dolphin South End Runners club in 1966, creating an environment that welcomed women, children and older adults at a time when many running organizations remained exclusive.

Phyllis Nabhan credits Stack with encouraging her to become involved in the sport.

"He said, I belong to the Dolphin South End Running Club and you need to join," Nabhan said.

She recalled the attention she received from a newspaper photographer during one race.

MORE: Here's what to know ahead of the 2026 SF Marathon

"This was my second Bay to Breakers and I don't know if the Examiner had cameras and I'm going 'hi' ha, ha, and they caught me in mid air, oh she is so animated, we'll put that in the newspaper," she said.

Journalist Ward Bushee, who wrote about Stack early in his career, said Stack's views on gender inclusion were ahead of their time.

"He was always very progressive and forward thinking about women and how they could be part of this recreational thing. You have to remember that this was before the Boston Marathon allowed women in the race," Bushee said.

The issue gained national attention in 1967 when Kathrine Switzer completed the Boston Marathon despite attempts by a race official to remove her from the course.

Less than a decade later, Joan Ullyot's 1976 book Women's Running challenged misconceptions about female athletes.

"She was so discriminated against in the 70s for running. The people would say women aren't supposed to run. Your uterus is going to fall out," Nabhan said.

MORE: BTS's Suga secretly runs Bay to Breakers in SF, finishes 12K before concert at Stanford

While many athletic organizations resisted change, Stack's running club welcomed a broad range of participants.

"That was really one of the main things about the DSE runners was that they wanted to be inclusive of women and kids, everybody and old people," said John Horner, president of the Dolphin Swim Club.

"Walt knew how good running was for both your body and your spirit," Horner added.

Although Stack's running club embraced women from the beginning, the Dolphin Swim Club and South End Rowing Club did not admit women until 1976, after a court ruling found that organizations operating on public land could not discriminate based on gender.

"He was a big proponent of people. He cared so much that everybody got to be who they could be, the best they could be and that he was inclusive, he included women in that algorithm so we all benefited from Walt's leadership," said Dolphin Swim Club member Diane Walton.

Stack's influence eventually extended far beyond the Bay Area.

MORE: South Bay runner invents radar-based wearable device to improve runner safety

In 1988, Nike selected the then-80-year-old runner as the first athlete featured in its new "Just Do It" advertising campaign.

"I run 17 miles every morning..." Stack said in the commercial.

The choice surprised many because Stack was not an elite professional athlete. Instead, he embodied the idea that running was for everyone.

"Of all the great athletes in the world, the first 'Just Do It' ad was Walt Stack piling along the Golden Gate Bridge with no shirt on, no teeth in," Bushee said.

In the advertisement, Stack became known for one of the campaign's most memorable lines.

"People ask me how I keep my teeth from chattering in the wintertime. I leave them in my locker," he said.

MORE: San Jose high school track coach launches program to help low-income kids run marathons

For many runners, the commercial demonstrated that athletic achievement was not limited by age or appearance.

"Waving at people, big kind of gut and just trolling along and it just meant so much, I think, in terms of bringing people together in terms of running to say, hey if he can do that, I can do that," Bushee said.

Today, younger runners may not recognize Stack's name, even as they benefit from the more inclusive running culture he helped create.

"The fact that women weren't allowed to join running clubs, how do you feel about that now? I mean that like is crazy now, there are so many women that run more like, back then definitely there weren't many opportunities for women to join running clubs," runner Sonya Ahmed said.

Asked about her own commitment to the sport, Ahmed said: "Yeah, definitely I feel like it's something that is an outlet for me, I run like almost every day."

Those who run across the Golden Gate Bridge today may be unaware of Stack's contributions to the local running movement, but those who knew him say his impact remains visible in every stride.

"I was lucky to know him as much as I did. I appreciate the inspiration that he gave to me and everybody else," Horner said.

title: Stock Up, Stock Down from New England’s Loss to the Cleveland Browns | Patriots Roundtable Podcast
description: The New England Patriots fell to the Cleveland Browns, 37-13, in the preseason finale. We review whose stock is up — and whose is down — as the cut down to 53 looms.
fullText:
Check out the Patriots Roundtable Podcast for more!

That's a wrap on the 2026 preseason.

Last night, New England Patriots traveled to Cleveland to take on the Browns in the preseason finale, falling by a score of 37-13. New England fell behind early in the game and failed to tighten the contest late as they focused more on rest and recovery than the result on Thursday night.

On today's episode of the Patriots Roundtable Podcast, hosts Eddie Marotta and Tyler Geis provide their key takeaways and review whose stock is up — and whose is down — after another competitive week of program installation and roster evaluation. Who made the most of their final audition and left a lasting impression as the cut down to 53 players looms? We debate whose case for inclusion on the regular season roster is irrefutable after a month of training camp, joint practices, and preseason games.

Offensively, second-year wide receiver Kyle Williams was one of a few lone bright spots for New England in the finale. He caught his third touchdown pass in as many preseason games in highlight-reel fashion, waltzing into the end zone from 45-yards out after beating former Patriot D'Angelo Ross on a signature go route down the left side line. Thursday was a much more efficient outing for Williams, who caught each of his two targets after hauling in just two-of-six last week. Williams, Tommy DeVito, and Caleb Lomu were among the New England players who only saw action in the first quarter, as the team rested 39 players to preserve health for the regular season opener on September 9.

Defensively, the Patriots struggled to keep Cleveland backup quarterbacks Dillion Gabriel and Taylen Green off the scoreboard and allowed points on each of the Browns' five first-half drives. Wide receiver Luke Floriea caught two touchdowns against New England depth cornerbacks in a very forgettable performance from Charles Woods and Kindle Vildor. Gabe Jacas played the first quarter but no longer, and once again had a difficult time reading option keepers and play-action fakes thrown at him by the opposition. Rookie linebacker Namdi Obiazor started the game and played into the fourth quarter, recording a game-high 11 tackles on the night.

New England's 2026 preseason is officially in the books. Now, the front office looks ahead to a collection of difficult decisions in the coming days, as the cut down to 53 must be completed by Sunday, August 30, at 6:00 p.m. ET.

Who stood out to you in the Patriots' preseason loss to the Browns? Who do you think survives the cut down to 53? Drop your thoughts in the comments below and join the conversation on Patriots Roundtable.

Follow the Patriots Roundtable Podcast!

title: Ravens practice squad projection before 53-man roster cuts
description: Projecting the Ravens' practice squad as cuts test Baltimore's depth at several positions
fullText:
The Ravens will have useful players left over when they reduce their roster to 53.

That makes the practice squad an important part of the next round of decisions. Baltimore needs players who can prepare the starters during the week, provide replacements when injuries occur, and continue to develop without a permanent spot on the active roster.

This projection follows the accompanying 53-man forecast. It includes 16 standard spots and C.J. Okoye as the projected additional international player. NFL rules allow the extra place when a qualifying player is designated, and Baltimore received an offseason exemption for Okoye via the NFL roster rules.

Players subject to waivers must clear before returning. Others can choose to sign elsewhere. These are projected signings, not assignments Baltimore can make unilaterally.

Another passer for practice work and injury coverage.

Backfield depth with kickoff return experience.

A receiver already familiar with the offense and return assignments.

Veteran depth for an otherwise young group of reserve receivers.

A right tackle option if the active roster carries only nine linemen.

Continued development without requiring an immediate game-day role.

Interior flexibility, including another option at center.

Time to develop behind the active guards.

Interior depth after a difficult numbers decision.

Another defensive line option for practice and future openings.

Continued evaluation if he clears waivers after missing the initial 53.

Edge depth behind a crowded active group.

Development at linebacker and on special teams.

A chance to continue his evaluation, subject to health and waiver clearance.

Additional coverage depth outside the projected top six corners.

An experienced replacement option behind the active safeties.

This forecast uses the additional international place for Okoye, provided Baltimore applies the designation when assembling the practice squad. It does not count both Okoye and Olajiga as exempt players.

Benny, Pounds and Isaac are among the players Baltimore could lose if another team offers an active-roster opportunity. Nick Dawkins, Ty Pezza, Lucas Scott, Michael Barrett and Silas Walters are other candidates. The Ravens could also sign players released elsewhere, particularly if those players address a need the current group does not.
