title: Reports split over whether forced contraception of Greenlandic women and girls constituted genocide
description: Two reports investigating the forcible contraception of thousands of Indigenous women and girls in Greenland by Danish health authorities for decades were split over whether the practice constituted g...
fullText:
NUUK, Greenland (AP) — Two reports investigating the forcible contraception of thousands of Indigenous women and girls in Greenland by Danish health authorities for decades were split over whether the practice constituted genocide.

The Greenlandic government, which commissioned the inquiry, released the reports Friday but, when pressed by journalists during a news conference, would not say whether its leaders concluded whether a genocide had occurred. The government told the authors to use the definition under the United Nations' 1948 genocide convention, which includes "imposing measures intended to prevent births within the group."

The reports come as U.S. President Donald Trump pushes to control the Arctic island, which is a self-governing territory of Denmark. The leaders of Greenland and Denmark say the island is not for sale and only Greenlanders can decide their fate.

Known as the "spiral case, " the revelations have rocked both Denmark and Greenland. More than 350 Greenlandic Indigenous women and girls, including some 12 years old and younger, previously came forward to investigators and reported that they were forcibly given contraception by Danish health authorities. Denmark says more than 4,000 women and girls — reportedly half the fertile women in Greenland at the time — received IUDs between the 1960s and mid-1970s.

The Inuit victims, many of them teenagers at the time, said they were either fitted with intrauterine contraceptive devices, known as IUDs or coils, or given a hormonal birth control injection. They were not told details about the procedure, or did not give their consent.

The alleged purpose was to limit population growth in Greenland by preventing pregnancies. The population on the Arctic island was rapidly increasing at the time because of better living conditions and better health care.

The cases occurred between the 1960s and the early 1990s. Greenland took over its own healthcare programs on Jan. 1, 1992.

The Danish government on Thursday approved payouts of 300,000 Danish kroner (about $46,500) to each victim. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen officially apologized last year.

Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said a reconciliation commission would be set up, a move that Frederiksen endorsed in a statement Friday.

On Friday, the Greenlandic government only accepted the findings of one of the reports, saying that an expert found that the second — the one that definitively said a genocide had not taken place — did not meet recognized scientific standards.

"There is no empirical evidence to assume that any Danish or Greenlandic authority, or any individual healthcare professional, at any time had any intention of destroying the Greenlandic population or a significant proportion of it," the authors of the rejected report wrote. "There was no genocide."

The accepted report, however, did not conclude whether there was a genocide. The authors wrote that they were not able to determine if any intent to destroy the population existed solely through the forcible contraception cases, and suggested further study that encompassed other Danish practices at the time that affected Greenlandic children and families. The authors did not, unlike the other report, conclusively say a genocide did not occur.

"It is difficult to imagine circumstances in which an attempt to substantially reduce the population of a single ethnic group could not constitute an intent to destroy, in part, that ethnicity," the report said.

The reports were originally supposed to be a single publication but two of the four members of the group broke away several months ago and wrote their own report. Theirs was the one rejected by the island's government; one of the authors is a former director of the Danish Institute for Human Rights.

"The reason given was professional disagreements amongst the members and, to some extent, concerns about the geopolitical situation," the Greenlandic government said Friday in a news release.

The news release did not elaborate on what the two authors considered to be the geopolitical situation.

title: Federal judge says Trump discussing payoff to Stormy Daniels isn’t an official presidential action
description: A federal judge again denied President Donald Trump’s legal effort to get his New York state criminal hush money case moved to federal court, a move that could have made it easier to reverse his convi...
fullText:
A federal judge again denied President Donald Trump's legal effort to get his New York state criminal hush money case moved to federal court, a move that could have made it easier to reverse his conviction.

District Judge Alvin Hellerstein said in a ruling Friday that Trump's cited grounds were "neither new nor legally sufficient."

Hellerstein has previously denied Trump's request to move the case, but a federal appellate court ruled last fall that the district court judge must reconsider in light of the landmark presidential immunity ruling in July 2024 from the US Supreme Court.

The judge heard arguments from lawyers for Trump and prosecutors from the Manhattan District Attorney's office at a hearing in February but did not issue a ruling until now. Friday, Hellerstein maintained his position that Trump's acts as charged in the state's case against him were private and unrelated to his federal office.

"The People's prosecution arises from President Trump's private conduct surrounding the reimbursement of hush money payments to an adult film star," Hellerstein wrote Friday. "That conduct, and the challenged evidence, bears no substantive relation to his position in federal office. To consider these facts to be 'relating to' a federal office would give the words a definition that is 'so broad that it is meaningless.'"

Trump immediately appealed Friday's ruling.

"The Supreme Court's historic decision on Immunity, the Federal and New York State Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed," a spokesman for Trump's legal team said in a statement.

Lawyers for Trump have appealed his 2024 criminal conviction on 34 counts of falsifying business records tied to hush money payments to adult film star Stormy Daniels during the 2016 presidential election. Their separate efforts to get the case moved to federal court started before the state trial, so a federal judge could interpret federal preemption and presidential immunity. The federal track would also offer a faster route for his appeal to get to the Supreme Court.

Despite the guilty finding, Trump was sentenced to unconditional discharge, meaning he faced no penalties and the conviction was essentially in name only. It did, however, make Trump the first president convicted of a felony.

Months after his conviction, his lawyers tried again in the wake of the immunity decision that said presidents are protected from criminal prosecution for official acts and barred prosecutors from attempting to enter evidence involving official acts, even if they were pursuing alleged crimes involving that president's private conduct.

Trump's defense team has long argued Trump can't be prosecuted in connection to the hush money scheme because he's protected by presidential immunity – he reimbursed his former personal attorney Michael Cohen while in office for a cover up scheme Cohen orchestrated during the 2016 election.

In his latest ruling, the judge wrote, "There is no way that discussions regarding hush money payments to cover up the President's relations with Stormy Daniels could be an official act. An affair, or a cover-up of an affair, is not within the "'outer perimeter' of the President's official responsibilities."

For Trump, the debate is whether Manhattan prosecutors improperly introduced evidence involving White House staffers' actions at the hush money trial that they allege was Trump's crimes as an individual separate from his capacity as president.

Hellerstein disagreed: "A president's assistant can work on unofficial, personal matters for the president."

Last November, the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals kicked the case back to Hellerstein and said the district court must reconsider but didn't weigh in on whether the SCOTUS decision should tip the scales for Trump.

Trump's lawyers also waited about two months to file that renewed request in federal court, first asking the state court Judge Juan Merchan to dismiss the conviction. Merchan denied the motion and Trump's appeal of his conviction is still moving through state appellate channels.

In February, Hellerstein called it a strategic decision to petition Merchan before the federal court. "You made a choice. You sought two bites at the apple," he said, signaling Friday's ruling back then.

In his order Friday, Hellerstein said Trump waited too long to file the renewed request for removal in federal court. "Trump's delay in filing for removal constitutes a "quintessential strategic decision," and the "fact that he later came to view that decision as a poor one is not sufficient, by itself, to establish cause."

The state appeal is also ongoing and could advance to the New York's Court of Appeals and potentially reach the US Supreme Court if Trump is unsuccessful at the lower appellate levels.

This story has been updated with additional details.

title: Strava Is Now Forcing Premium Users to See Its AI Workout Summaries (Whether They Want to or Not)
description: It used to be optional; now, it's not.
fullText:
You can’t turn off Strava’s AI summaries anymore. Sometime in July or August, the feature, called “Athlete Intelligence,” became a built-in part of premium subscriptions. If you have a free account, you still won’t see it, but if you 

Athlete Intelligence, conveniently abbreviated AI, is a Strava feature that gives text responses to your workouts. It’s only available for premium subscribers. Strava refers to “insights” in these responses, but as far as I can tell, they just seem to regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors.

I used the feature briefly, around the time it launched (I was a premium subscriber then), but quickly turned it off when I realized it wasn’t telling me anything interesting. I asked my colleague Meredith Dietz, who has a premium subscription, whether she had seen anything useful in her Athlete Intelligence. She said, “They’re usually positive, so that’s nice. But ultimately: useless.”

Meredith has written more about why AI fitness summaries are mostly useless, and Strava’s AI checks every box: it doesn’t use enough context to understand what’s going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it’s overconfident in its incomplete data. She showed me a recent Athlete Intelligence summary that said a run was both a “recovery run” and included her “fastest pace in two weeks.” Those are simply not compatible statements. Another message complimented her “solid half-marathon effort” on a run that Meredith says was “not even close to a half-marathon effort.”

You used to be able to turn off the AI. When Strava launched Athlete Intelligence in October 2024, it was a “beta” feature available to premium users only. Since then—as far as I can remember—Strava’s support page had instructions for opting out of Athlete Intelligence.

But that changed recently. The last Wayback Machine snapshot that included those instructions is from June 30, 2026. A snapshot from Aug. 4 removed both the question and answer about opting out. On Aug. 26, I noticed a Reddit thread where users were wondering where the opt-out feature went. The support page currently says, “There isn’t an option to opt out of Athlete Intelligence.”

I asked what happened, and received an answer from a Strava spokesperson: “As was standard practice for experimental features, Athlete Intelligence launched with a "turn off" mechanism scoped to its initial beta period. Given the feature’s formal exit from beta, that mechanism is no longer available. We invite all subscribers to tap Give Feedback to help us improve the insights they see.”

Athlete Intelligence officially left beta in February of last year. If the support page was kept up to date over the subsequent year and a half, then it seems the opt-out was removed much later. (The instructions used to say to click “leave beta” and then changed to “leave Athlete Intelligence” sometime before June 21 this year.) I asked Strava for clarification on the timeline, and got the answer: “Thanks for the follow up, we're not able to provide additional information.”

Strava claimed in its February 2025 announcement that over 80% of users found Athlete Intelligence useful. That seems hard to believe, given the weaknesses that both Meredith and I noticed in our own AI summaries. For all my browsing of Strava user forums, I’ve often seen people complaining about the AI’s tone or pointing out its mistakes; I’m really not seeing anyone praising it for being insightful or for helping to analyze or plan training.

Meredith finds the summaries easy to ignore. I found they annoyed me, so I hid them while it was still possible to do so. So far I’m not seeing anybody who opted out complaining that the summaries are back; it’s possible they will remain hidden. But the option to turn them off is no longer available. You can still “leave feedback” on a given response, but there used to be an option to leave Athlete Intelligence altogether. That option is no longer there, and given Strava’s statement, it doesn’t seem likely it will come back.

title: 10 Hacks Every Intel Mac User Should Know
description: If you're rocking an older machine, here are some tips to keep it running well.
fullText:
When macOS 27 drops next month, Apple will officially say goodbye to its Intel-based Macs. The only Macs that will be able to update to macOS Golden Gate next month will be the ones with an Apple-made chip (including the A18 Pro on the MacBook Neo). Yet while Apple hasn't sold an Intel Mac in quite some time, there are still plenty of them in existence. You might even still use an Intel Mac as your daily driver.

While I can't say enough good things about Apple silicon, I also strongly believe in using your tech as long as it keeps working for you. As such, if you're rocking one of Apple's older Macs, whether that's a MacBook, a Mac mini, or an iMac, you should check out these hacks and tips to get the most out of your machine—and, hopefully, put off having to upgrade it for quite some time.

Your Intel Mac may support Apple's latest software version as of this writing, which is macOS 26. But if you've had it a while, it likely doesn't—in fact, it may not natively support the last two or three macOS versions prior to that. That's where OpenCore Legacy Patcher comes in. This project bypasses Apple's restrictions to install macOS versions on devices the company no longer officially supports. The idea isn't to force an aging Mac to struggle to run a newer version of macOS, either: Many machines are perfectly capable of running macOS versions that Apple doesn't officially support, so users may be pleasantly surprised by their performance.

Unfortunately, OpenCore Legacy Patcher is itself becoming a legacy product. Now that Apple has dropped Intel, it might not be possible for a system like OpenCore to hack macOS 27 onto your Mac. At this time, macOS Sequoia is the latest version OpenCore supports, so you can't upgrade to macOS 26 Tahoe or macOS 27 Golden Gate. Still, you can use the platform to get your Mac running something a bit more recent, which may increase both third-party software support as well as your security. Your experience will depend on your specific Mac model, so follow OpenCore's instructions to get started.

The good news is, even if you can't run the latest version of macOS on your machine, you may still be able to run the latest versions of the apps that really matter: Apple is still updating the Safari app for older versions of macOS, as are many third-party app developers. What's more, Apple still releases security patches for some older macOS versions, so even if your Intel Mac doesn't have all the latest features, it may still be protected against the latest vulnerabilities.

If your Intel Mac has fans, and if you've never cleaned them, fix that. Your Mac's fans are designed to keep its internal components cool by pushing hot air away from your machine. The longer it can keep components from heating up too much, the longer you can push your Mac without running into performance throttling—or, in other words, the longer your Mac can run at peak performance. Over time, dust works its way inside your fans, reducing their ability to move air properly. After years, your fans might not be able to move hot air efficiently. Luckily, this isn't hard to fix.

To clean your Mac's fans, you'll need to open up your machine to access them. How you do this will depend on your specific Mac model. (iMacs can be particularly difficult to open, as you need to remove the display entirely.) To find instructions for your model, look up your specific device on iFixit, as the site will likely have both walkthroughs as well as the tools you'll need to perform the operation.

Once they're clean, make sure your fans are cooling your Mac to its fullest. While macOS sets fan speeds on its own based on how you use your Mac, you can install a program like Macs Fan Control to unlock direct control of your Mac's fans. You can push them to their limits if you want maximum cooling, or simply monitor your Mac's overall temperatures. I used to use this program all the time to maintain high performance on my Intel MacBook: Without it, I noticed my Mac slowing down during more intense sessions. With it, I was able to push it much harder.

If your Mac is very old, you might actually be able to "hack" it to make it work better. For the past 14 years or so, Apple has had an obsession with gluing and soldering all its components together, making it impossible to upgrade any of them individually. But older machines used to come with modular parts that users could upgrade themselves. Notably, that included the RAM and the hard drive. If you install extra memory, your Mac may be able to run more programs and processes at once without slowing things down; if your Mac has a physical hard drive, adding an SSD will massively boost startup and loading times. Of course, prices for those components may have increased beyond financial viability thanks to the global memory crisis.

Still, if your MacBook or iMac falls into this category, you should definitely look into upgrading it. The newest MacBook that supports upgradable RAM is from 2012, but the latest iMac is only from 2020. You'll find Apple's official instructions at both of those links. The company doesn't appear to have support guides for replacing Mac hard drives these days, but Google your Mac model, and, if one exists, you should find replacement guides from sources like iFixit.

If you're rocking an Intel-based MacBook and you've never replaced its battery, it's likely time for an update. Lithium-ion batteries don't last forever, and as they degrade, their overall capacity diminishes. Let's say your battery currently has a maximum capacity of 75%. That means once you charge it up to 100%, it's like you only charged it to 75% relative to when it was new. By replacing your battery, you're giving your MacBook its life back—at least, its battery life.

Now, how easy your battery replacement is will depend on your MacBook's model. Again, very old MacBooks are much easier to work on, so your biggest challenge may just be finding a replacement battery. If your old MacBook is on the newer side, you might find a battery more easily, but replacing it may be more difficult. As such, it might make sense to take it to a repair shop—assuming the cost of repair isn't comparable to the cost of a new MacBook. For this hack, search the web for your specific MacBook model and battery replacement—a site like iFixit almost assuredly has a guide, including parts you can purchase.

Installing a new battery isn't the only way to keep your old Mac up and running for longer. Even if your Mac doesn't support an official Low Power Mode, you can download TurboBoostSwitcher to save on power. Here's how it works: Intel chips have what's called "Turbo Boost," which kicks in when the system thinks you need more power than usual. That's great for performance, but bad for your battery life—especially if you prioritize your battery over power. In addition, too much Turbo Boost can cause your Mac to run hot, which may cause the system to throttle performance to cool things down—defeating Turbo Boost's purpose entirely.

TurboBoostSwitcher gives you a manual switch to disable Turbo Boost when you want to save on power. When you do, the chip never pushes itself in times of stress—so while you may notice things running a bit more slowly, you should also notice your battery lasting a bit longer. This was my go-to back when my Intel MacBook was my main machine, and I'm happy to see it's still available.

If you need access to Windows for work or personal use but only have an Intel Mac lying around, you don't need to go out and buy a new PC. Because your Mac has an Intel chip, you can actually install and run Windows natively on your machine, through an official Mac process called Boot Camp. With Boot Camp, you "partition" a selection of your Mac's hard drive for Windows: Perhaps you give it 100GB, enough to install the OS as well as store files on the system itself. Whatever you choose, when you boot up your Mac, you'll be able to select either macOS or Windows, and boot into it. While Apple hasn't sold an Intel Mac for years, it still has an official Boot Camp guide you can follow to get started.

I'll always have a soft spot for the Touch Bar. While I admit the company could have made some better choices with it—including adding a row of physical function keys below it—I always like the Touch Bar, and I enjoyed using it to adjust controls. The few apps that actually took advantage of the Touch Bar's functionality were useful too, but for the most part, the feature felt underbaked or even counterintuitive.

Still, if your MacBook has a Touch Bar, there are ways to "hack" it to your advantage. There are system settings to adjust, but you can go further than Apple's own settings (which the company has long moved on from). Using an app called BetterTouchTool, you can customize how your Touch Bar looks and works, and add functions like widgets and gestures. The app lets you customize a host of things on your Mac beyond the Touch Bar, but I was originally introduced to it for the purposes of Touch Bar hacking. If your Mac has a Touch Bar, give it a shot.

Storage is a precious commodity. Hard drives are more expensive than ever, so taking advantage of any available storage should be a priority. As such, if you don't need to use your old Mac for much these days, treat it like an external drive. Depending on your Mac model, you may have as much storage as you'd buy with a dedicated drive. My old Touch Bar MacBook, for example, has a 512GB drive, so I use it as a backup for some of my important files—especially videos. Sure, you could recycle your old Mac to save on clutter, but if you need an external drive anyway, you may already have one in your machine.

If you don't intend to use your Mac as intended any longer, don't give it away. Instead, you can use it passively to power a home media server. These servers effectively let you customize your own Netflix: You add the digital media you own (movies, shows, music, photos, etc.), then set up the server on your Mac. Done properly, you'll be able to access your content from any device, from anywhere you have an internet connection. You can watch shows on your TV streamed from your Mac, or listen to music while on a trip, remotely connecting back to your machine at home. To get started, you can use a service like Plex. However, Plex is just one of many such platforms; others include Emby, Jellyfin, and Kodi.

title: 10 Spotlight Search Hacks Every Mac User Should Know
description: Spotlight Search can do much, much more than just finding files and apps.
fullText:
Spotlight search is one of the most useful features in macOS. You can access it by pressing Command-Space, and it allows you to find anything on your Mac. And there's so much more Spotlight search can do than you might realize. From performing currency conversions to running complex automation routines, here are 10 Spotlight search hacks that you'll find useful.

Since the release of macOS 26 Tahoe, Spotlight search has been able to store your clipboard history. This means that Spotlight keeps a record of every item you copy on your Mac. This feature is disabled by default. You can enable it by clicking the Apple logo in the top-left corner of your Mac's screen, and going to System Settings > Spotlight. Scroll down, and enable Results from Clipboard. You can use the drop-down menu below this option to set an auto-delete timer for clipboard history, and your choices are 30 minutes, 8 hours, or 7 days.

To access clipboard history, press Command-Space to open Spotlight search, and then, press Command-4.

I stopped using online searches for currency and unit conversions ever since I discovered this Spotlight feature. To convert currency in Spotlight search, you can type "USD 100 to INR." The result appears in Spotlight, which is a lot faster than opening a browser and performing a web search. Feel free to replace the currency abbreviations with the ones you need, as Spotlight search supports almost all countries' currencies (but not cryptocurrencies). You can use similar syntax to convert units. For example, try something like: "100lbs to kg," or "3L to oz."

You should also try Spotlight's built-in calculator, which can handle arithmetic quite well. Ask it to add, subtract, divide, or multiply numbers, and Spotlight will show you the results instantly.

Once you have the search bar open, you can type any file name or app name, and Spotlight will search your Mac to locate it—that part is pretty clear. The fun begins when you start using search filters for advanced queries. You can ask Spotlight to restrict search results to PDF files by typing "/pdf" ahead of your query. This works for other file types such as jpeg, png, and tiff. To use it correctly, you'll have to select the filter from the search results. When you type "/pdf," the first search result will be "PDF" with the word Kind written under it. Select this, and type your query to restrict queries to that file type.

You can also use this format to search specific folders, such as "/downloads" to look for files in the Downloads folder in your Mac.

Whenever I open any chat app with the intention of messaging someone, I get distracted by other unread messages. To avoid this on my Mac, I've started messaging people directly from Spotlight, which lets me avoid looking at unrelated messages. To use this feature, open Spotlight, and type "Send Message." You can select the Send Message action from the results to start composing the text. You can then pick a recipient and hit the Return key to send the message.

Your Mac's built-in Clock app lets you set alarms, timers, or use a stopwatch. This works fine, but when I'm setting timers, I usually want to do it fast. That's where Spotlight comes in. Type "Start Timer" and select the action in Spotlight. You can then add a duration for the timer, and it'll alert you when time's up.

When I see search results in Spotlight, sometimes I want to open the file or app, but more often than not, I want to open the folder that contains those results. I recently discovered a keyboard shortcut that opens the folder containing any search result directly from Spotlight. To use it, look for something in Spotlight search, and use the arrow keys to reach the correct result. Then press Command-Enter to open the file or app in Finder.

I had no idea that Spotlight could also be your personal translator, until Lifehacker's Senior Technology Editor Jake Peterson told me about it. Now that I've used the feature, I don't think I'll be opening Google Translate by default when I need translations. To set up this feature on your Mac, go to System Settings > Language & Region, and select Translation Languages. Download the languages you need to translate, and enable On-Device Mode on the same page if you want offline translations. Click Done when all downloads are complete.

Once this is done, type "Translate" in Spotlight, and select the Translate Text action from the results. Type or paste some text into the "Text" field, and Spotlight will show you the translation shortly.

Ever since macOS switched away from the old System Preferences menu, I've had trouble locating many settings on my MacBook. The new System Settings menu is less confusing for iOS users, but that doesn't help those of us who were used to the old layout. To get around this, I've started using Spotlight search to find system settings. You can type the name of the settings page, or even specific features such as Reduce Motion. Spotlight's results will show you two types of results: One where you can open the System Settings app, and the other where you can toggle the preference directly from search results. The latter is especially handy for features you want to toggle more than once, such as Bluetooth.

Now that Spotlight search lets you run actions such as creating notes, calendar events, and sending messages, it's worth considering ways to speed up this process. Typing the full name of each action isn't a good solution for actions you use frequently, which is why it's a good idea to assign keyboard shortcuts to your favorite actions. Instead of typing "Send Message" each time, you could trigger the action by typing "sm." To set this up, open Spotlight and press Command-3. This will load the list of actions supported by all installed apps on your Mac, and you can click the "Add quick keys" button next to any action to assign a keyboard shortcut.

If you don't want to see results from certain apps in Spotlight search, you can exclude those apps easily. On your Mac, go to System Settings > Spotlight, and scroll down to the "Results from Apps" section. You can click the button next to any app to remove it from Spotlight results. Scroll down further till you reach the "Results from System" section. Here, you can click the i button next to "Files" and exclude certain folders from Spotlight search results.

title: Alexander surges clear at Women's Irish Open
description: Two eagles propels overnight leader Casandra Alexander to a second-round 66 as the South African seizes control of the Women's Irish Open at the K Club.
fullText:
Women's Irish Open - second round

-15 C Alexander (SA); -10 B Navarossa (US), S Kouskova (Cze); -9 L Rydqvist (Swe), C Viden (Swe); -8 L Pettersson (Swe); -7 A Foersterling (Ger); -5 P Urs (Ind), A Fanali (Ita); N Komulainen (Fin), C Screene (Ire).

Selected others: -4 L M Humphreys (Eng), A Hewson (Eng); -3 A Dawson (IoM), G Clews (Eng), H Darling (Sco), L Hall (Wal) -2 L Maguire (Ire), A Donegan (Ire); -1 A Foster (Ire), A Wilson (NI); +4 O Mehaffey (NI)

Two eagles propelled overnight leader Casandra Alexander to a second-round 66 as the South African seized control of the Women's Irish Open at the K Club.

Following a bogey-free 63 on Thursday, Alexander eagled the par-five 10th - her opening hole - on Friday and followed that with back-to-back birdies.

Having dropped a shot on 13, the 27-year-old carded a birdie two on 17 before recording her second eagle of the round at the third.

After a bogey on six, a birdie on seven gave Alexander a 36-hole total of 129 to sit five shots clear of the Czech Republic's Sara Kouskova (68) and American Brianna Navarrosa (65).

Canice Screene leads the home challenge as she lies in a four-way tie for eighth on five under after mixing seven birdies with two bogeys in a five-under 67, but Aine Donegan slipped back to two under with a disappointing 73.

After opening with a 71, Leona Maguire reached four under for the tournament but bogeyed two of her last three holes to fall back to two under at the halfway mark.

title: How will Scottish clubs respond to Euro disappointments?
description: Read the best storylines before this weekend's full card of Scottish Premiership fixtures.
fullText:
The Scottish Premiership returns for 10 clubs this weekend after only two sides played last time out.

Five clubs were given more time to prepare for European play-off fixtures and, while Hearts succeeded in their task of progression, Rangers, Hibernian and Motherwell all missed out on the Conference League.

Celtic crumbled in the second leg of their Champions League play-off against LASK, although they have the compensation of still being in Europe in the Europa League.

Those midweek results beg questions before Saturday and Sunday's games.

Celtic face Benfica & Hearts meet Trabzonspor

Have expensively assembled Rangers improved at all under McInnes?

Until Tuesday, champions Celtic's season was ambling along well. Three domestic wins without conceding and a 3-0 victory over LASK in the first leg of the Champions League play-off had them in good stead.

Their position improved further with the opening goal in the second leg in Austria. Four LASK goals later, it was extra time. And then, the tie was lost as a fifth concession on the night consigned Celtic to the Europa League.

They will face Benfica, Bestikas, Celta Vigo, Ferencvaros, Marseille, Omonia, Torreense and Union SG in the autumn but, before then, they have domestic matters to turn to, starting with a home match with Falkirk on Saturday (15:00 BST).

Celtic's form pre-Austria and their record of five wins out of five against Falkirk last season would suggest this game should hold no fears for them but could a European hangover beset the Premiership holders?

Captain Callum McGregor said they were "passive" and looked "scared" against the Austrian champions. Indeed, the way in which the tie got away from Celtic was alarming.

Martin O'Neill side played 120 minutes during the week while Falkirk are refreshed after two weeks without a game.

Despite that, John McGlynn's side await a first league win this season and face an almighty task to get one in Glasgow.

Dundee were one of the teams Celtic beat earlier in the season, but narrowly.

Since then, in the Premiership, Steven Pressley's side have taken big strides with 2-0 wins over Aberdeen at home and away to city rivals Dundee United, though a cup loss to Aberdeen was sandwiched in between.

St Mirren are the only team other than Celtic with a 100% record in the league so far after two wins out of two against Falkirk away and St Johnstone at home. The Buddies sustained a heavy loss in their League Cup tie away to Rangers, ending their hopes of defending that trophy.

Both Dundee and St Mirren should be refreshed after no midweek action, with the latter having had last weekend off too.

And, on Sunday at 15:00, they host Hibernian and Motherwell, respectively - two sides coming off midweek European exits.

Motherwell were already up against it away to Freiburg, who completed a 7-2 aggregate win to progress in the Conference League but Hibs endured a painful play-off exit at the hands of Gent, losing 3-2 after the Belgians scored two late goals.

It may be a good time for Dundee and St Mirren to be meeting these teams.

Sunday's fixture card starts with the 12:00 meeting of Aberdeen and Rangers, often a feisty affair. For added spice, Rangers manager Derek McInnes is of course a former Aberdeen boss and is having rather a torrid time.

Still waiting for a league win and knocked out of two European competitions, McInnes faces quite the task in getting his newly assembled squad ready for the trip to Pittodrie.

The Dons, on the other hand, have their tails up after an opening league win against last season's runners-up Hearts and a solid cup win against Dundee.

Neither side were in action last weekend but Stephen Robinson's Aberdeen will be the more refreshed team, with Rangers having had a long night in the Czech Republic on Thursday.

A painful defeat on penalties by Jablonec ended their European interest this season and confidence seems to be low.

Not only that, it remains unclear both what the manager's preferred starting XI and preferred formation are.

It's yet another test for McInnes early in his Ibrox tenure.

title: Huddersfield upset Leigh with five-try win
description: Huddersfield Giants score five tries to upset in-form Leigh and keep the Leopards waiting to secure their place in the Super League play-offs.
fullText:
Tries: Rushton, Milne, Evalds, Geyer 2 Goals: Flanagan 5

Tries: Trout, Hanley, Mulhern Goals: Cook 3

Huddersfield Giants scored five tries to upset in-form Leigh and keep the Leopards waiting to secure their place in the Super League play-offs.

Leigh scored the night's first try through Owen Trout but tries from Harry Rushton and Taane Milne helped put Huddersfield 14-6 ahead at half-time.

Niall Evalds extended the lead after the break before Leigh's Umyla Hanley and Huddersfield's Cole Geyer exchanged tries as the Giants remained ahead.

Robbie Mulhern's try kept Leigh alive with 11 minutes to play but Geyer's second score with six minutes remaining sealed an impressive victory for Huddersfield.

Victory for Huddersfield was their seventh of the season, with five of those victories coming in their past six matches, and moved them up to 12th in the table and above York ahead of their trip to Toulouse.

Leigh arrived having won eight of their past nine games and victory would have secured their place in the top six.

They remain fifth and are still well-placed to reach the play-offs with two games remaining after St Helens, in seventh, lost at home to Leeds.

The visitors scored the opening try after nine minutes as Trout claimed an up-and-under and reached out to score.

But Huddersfield responded with 14 points in 10 minutes before half-time.

Rushton barged over before George Flanagan kicked a penalty from in front of the posts and then Tui Lolohea's high kick was spilled by Leigh's Innes Senior and the ball fell for Milne to run in.

Leeds go back top with thumping win at St Helens

Catalans beat Tigers after delay for power outage

Leading 14-6 at the start of the second half, Zac Woolford broke from dummy half and found Evalds to score Huddersfield's third try.

Needing a response, Leigh released Josh Charnley up the right wing and sent Hanley over on his 100th Super League appearance.

But Huddersfield forced a goal-line drop-out that was taken short, Giants claimed the kick and they drove towards the line before Woolford grubbered in-goal for Geyer to dot down.

Leigh kept themselves alive again as they reclaimed the restart, were immediately in behind the defence and sent Mulhern over from the next play.

But they soon knocked on to give Huddersfield field position and Geyer found a gap to slide in for his second try to seal the game.

Leigh head coach Adrian Lam told BBC Radio Manchester:

"It was hard to watch and nothing like we've been over the past four months.

"I thought Huddersfield were great, they were very physical and on point and we knew we were going to come here and have a tough game.

"We knew we needed to be sharp with high completions and minimum errors and we just came out of that really badly and it's the worst we've played over the last three-four months."

Leigh: O'Brien; Senior, Badrock, Hanley, Charnley; Cook, Lam; Ofahengaue, Horne, Mulhern, Hughes, Trout, Liu

Interchanges: Brogan, Ashworth, Alick-Wiencke, Ipape

title: Groom seeks helicopter from wedding to play at Lord's
description: Peter Melhuish needs to captain his cricket team less than 24 hours after he ties the knot.
fullText:
A groom is trying to secure a helicopter ride so he can play in a dream cricket match at Lord's immediately after his wedding in North Wales.

Peter Melhuish, from Guildford in Surrey, is due to play at Lord's on 6 September for his club Blackheath after they made it to the final of the Cawston Press Village Cup.

But the team captain is marrying his fiancée, Izzy Upton, in North Wales less than 24 hours earlier.

The couple, both 32, planned their wedding for the Saturday after Blackheath's local league fixtures finished for the season.

However, they did not factor in the club's success in the Village Cup, a nationwide tournament played on Sundays by local teams across the UK.

Now, Melhuish's clubmates are trying to raise around £9,000 so the pair can make the one-hour flight from North Wales to London by the game's 11:00 BST start.

"It'd be amazing if we can afford it and pull something together," said Melhuish.

"The only other way is a 5am taxi down from the wedding which wouldn't be much fun.

"It's amazing how the club are pulling together and helping us with it.

"It's really nice to have that support from them," he added.

Blackheath - which Melhuish first joined aged six - has entered the Village Cup since the tournament was first launched in 1972.

Melhuish added his fiancée Izzy had been "great".

"We've been organising the wedding for well over a year so the fixtures for the Village Cup hadn't even come out when we started organising it.

"She's been really supportive and very understanding of how much it means, not just to me but the club too," he continued.

title: Injury uncertainty led to 'intrusive thoughts' for Alcaraz
description: Seven-time major champion Carlos Alcaraz says not knowing when he would be able to return from a wrist injury was most challenging part of his long absence.
fullText:
Seven-time major champion Carlos Alcaraz says dealing with "intrusive thoughts" over when he would be able to return from his wrist injury was the most challenging part of his long absence.

Spain's Alcaraz, 23, has not played a singles match since mid-April but says he feels "great" as he prepares to make his comeback at the US Open, which begins in New York on Sunday.

Alcaraz, who beat rival Jannik Sinner in last year's final at Flushing Meadows, starts his title defence against powerful Russian Roman Safiullin in a contest which is likely to examine his lack of competitive action.

"Once I started to practice a little bit but didn't know when I'm going to [return], those thoughts were really difficult to deal with," said Alcaraz.

"I didn't know if I was going to be ready for Cincinnati, for the US Open, or [if] I'm going to miss the whole American swing.

"That was really difficult to deal with, but finally here we are. Those intrusive thoughts were the most difficult things to deal with in this process."

Why tough US Open draw will be true test of Alcaraz's fitness

How to follow US Open on the BBC

Alcaraz made his return to a match court at the US Open earlier this week, when he played alongside 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams in the mixed doubles event.

Alcaraz, who won the New York title in 2022 and 2025, continues to wear a compression sleeve on his playing arm in a bid to protect his wrist.

Wrist injuries are notoriously problematic for tennis players - and taking a gamble when an issue arises in this delicate area can be very costly.

Alcaraz has needed to show patience as he dealt with what is thought to be tenosynovitis, where the sheath that protects the tendon on the inside of the wrist becomes inflamed.

Alcaraz generates huge amounts of power through his forehand, which puts a lot of load through the joint of his playing wrist.

But speaking on Friday, he insists he feels mentally ready to compete in five-set matches at the highest level.

"It's really challenging. Probably, you know, in terms of preparation and everything, it is not the best time," said Alcaraz, who will be seeded second at the tournament despite his extended lay-off.

"But we, my team and me, believe that I'm ready."

He added: "I've got to trust my team, I've got to trust my people that tell me it's going be fine.

"I just have to go 100%, and right now I think with the practices I have done so far, it's been all good.

"I'm trying to stay away from any fear and I'm playing normal."

title: What will Jackson bring to Villa with Watkins set for exit?
description: BBC Sport examines what new striker Nicolas Jackson will bring to Aston Villa, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Al-Hilal.
fullText:
Aston Villa have completed the signing of Nicolas Jackson in a deal worth up to £65m, with Ollie Watkins looking set to join Saudi Pro League side Al-Hilal.

Unai Emery's Villa are undergoing a major overhaul this summer, with key players including Morgan Rogers, Ezri Konsa, Youri Tielemans and Lucas Digne having already departed.

Jackson, 25, joins a number of new additions including Johan Manzambi, Joao Gomes, Zion Suzuki and Matteo Ruggeri.

That level of squad disruption was evident on the opening weekend, when Emery's side slumped to a 4-0 defeat at Brighton.

With Watkins, 30, unavailable and both Tammy Abraham and 17-year-old Brian Madjo injured, Villa started without a recognised centre-forward - Emiliano Buendia led the line.

The arrival of Jackson - who overtakes Manzambi to become Villa's record signing - from Chelsea gives Emery a specialist striker to work with.

It also looks set to coincide with the end of Watkins' six-year spell at Villa, during which he scored 108 goals in 278 games and became one of the defining players of the rise under Emery.

However, the stats suggest Jackson is not just a like-for-like replacement for the England international - he is a different type of number nine.

On the surface, Jackson's numbers at Bayern Munich last season compare favourably with those of Watkins at Villa.

The Senegal forward scored 11 goals and provided three assists in 1,320 minutes across all competitions, averaging 1.0 goal involvements per 90 minutes. Watkins recorded 21 goals and five assists in 3,837 minutes, an average of 0.6 per 90.

Jackson also generated more attacking opportunities. He averaged 3.8 shots per 90 compared with Watkins' 2.6, and 2.2 shots on target to 1.2.

His expected-goals (xG) figure was also higher, at 0.7 per 90 compared with 0.5, while he averaged 8.5 touches in the opposition box to Watkins' 5.6.

That fits a pattern which predates his spell in Germany. Among players with at least 5,000 Premier League minutes since January 2020, only Erling Haaland has registered a higher non-penalty xG figure per 90 than Jackson's 0.55.

Getting into scoring positions has rarely been Jackson's main problem - it is his ability to finish chances which has attracted scrutiny.

During his two Premier League seasons with Chelsea, he scored 14 goals from 18.7 xG in 2023-24 and 10 from 12.3 xG the following campaign.

Jackson has converted 18 of 61 big chances in England so far, although Watkins has also missed plenty of high-value opportunities (scoring 24 of 73 since joining Villa in 2020).

Interestingly, last season's numbers suggest the gap between them was negligible. Jackson converted 19.6% of his shots and 40.9% of his big chances, compared with 18.9% and 43.2% respectively for Watkins.

There is, however, an important caveat.

Watkins started 43 matches and played almost three times as many minutes. Jackson started only 15 of his 34 appearances, and Opta says his relatively limited, substitute-heavy sample could make some of his per-90 figures look stronger than they might over a full season.

Both players were predominantly used as centre-forwards last season, making the comparison reasonably fair.

Watkins played 100% of his 3,837 minutes as a striker, with 92% coming as the central striker in Villa's 4-2-3-1.

Jackson spent 95% of his 1,320 minutes up front, with the remaining 5% on the left. At Bayern, 86% of his playing time came as the striker in a 4-2-3-1.

The similarity largely ends there. Jackson averaged 46.6 open-play touches per 90, compared with Watkins' 29.5, and completed almost twice as many passes - 24 per 90 to Watkins' 11.6.

He was also considerably more involved in creating and progressing attacks. Jackson averaged:

1.6 shot-ending carries per 90, compared with Watkins' 0.8

1.6 successful take-ons per 90, compared with 0.82

2.5 passes into the penalty area per 90, compared with 0.7.

Opta's touch maps reinforce the difference. Watkins' involvement was concentrated more heavily around the centre of the final third and penalty area, while Jackson received possession across a wider range of attacking zones.

Among a sample of 1,577 top-five European league strikers over the past 10 seasons, Jackson ranked in the 85th percentile for chances created, 77th for progressive carries and 73rd for touches.

Watkins ranked in the 28th, 53rd and eighth percentiles respectively. That points towards Villa moving from a relatively low-touch focal point to a forward who is more comfortable becoming involved in attacks earlier.

There is another possible difference when Villa lose possession. Jackson averaged 34 high pressures per 90, slightly above Watkins' 31.4, but the distinction becomes clearer in where possession was recovered.

Jackson won the ball 2.7 times per 90, compared with Watkins' 1.8, and regained it in the final third 0.9 times per 90 to Watkins' 0.6.

His percentile for possession won in the attacking third was 88th among the Opta striker sample, compared with Watkins' 43rd.

The two were almost identical for runs in behind, Jackson averaging 13 per 90 and Watkins 12.7, although the Englishman made slightly more runs which finished inside the penalty area.

Watkins also offered more aerially, winning 1.2 aerial duels per 90 compared with Jackson's 0.7, and carried the ball more directly towards goal. So Jackson would not necessarily reproduce every aspect of the player he is replacing.

Villa's interest also comes with an element of familiarity. Emery worked with Jackson at Villarreal, where the forward made 27 appearances under him, scoring three goals and providing three assists in 1,195 minutes.

Jackson has subsequently credited Emery with transforming his understanding of the game.

"Unai taught me everything about football," he said,

Jackson has explained that, when he arrived from Senegal, he possessed natural dribbling ability but had much less understanding of how and when to move.

Emery helped turn that instinctive talent into a more structured game.

Jackson's development accelerated after Emery left Villarreal. During the 2022-23 La Liga season he produced 0.56 non-penalty xG plus xA per 90, a rate bettered by only seven players with at least 1,500 minutes, all representing Barcelona, Real Madrid or Atletico Madrid.

Jackson's ability to carry the ball was already evident too. Ten of his league goal involvements followed carries, fewer only than Vinicius Jr, despite Jackson playing substantially fewer minutes.

Chelsea subsequently signed him in 2023. He scored 30 goals and supplied 12 assists in 81 appearances for the club before spending last season on loan at Bayern.

His time in Munich was complicated by circumstances rather than simply performance.

Bayern's obligation to buy would have been triggered if he reached a demanding appearance threshold, but Harry Kane remained fit and prolific, while the displays of Luis Diaz and Michael Olise limited opportunities elsewhere across the frontline.

Jackson still produced 11 goals across all competitions, and only Kane recorded a better rate of open-play Bundesliga goals per 90.

Bayern coach Vincent Kompany publicly defended him when criticism resurfaced, pointing to the quality of the forwards ahead of him and saying Jackson had trained and performed well.

Watkins has provided Villa with reliability, running power and goals throughout one of the club's most successful periods of the modern era.

Jackson arrives with a different profile. He is five years younger, gets more touches, carries the ball more frequently, creates more for others and, in limited minutes last season, generated shots and high-quality chances at an impressive rate.

There remain questions around whether those per-90 numbers would survive a heavier workload, while his finishing record at Chelsea explains why doubts have followed him.

But Villa are not buying an unknown quantity. Emery has coached Jackson before, knows the qualities he wants to develop and would be replacing a 30-year-old striker with a 25-year-old whose underlying numbers suggest there may still be considerable room to improve.

If Jackson joins and Watkins does depart, the Europa League winners will be doing more than just changing their centre-forwards.

They will be changing the way their number nine plays.

title: Mayer and Cameron butt heads at final face-off
description: Mikaela Mayer and Chantelle Cameron butt heads in their final face-off before Saturday's light-middleweight unification bout in Birmingham.
fullText:
Mikaela Mayer and Chantelle Cameron butted heads in their final face-off before Saturday's light-middleweight unification bout in Birmingham.

WBA and WBC champion Mayer and Briton Cameron had been cordial during the build-up but tensions spilled over at Friday's weigh-in.

As the pair came together to face-off at BP Pulse Arena, Cameron pushed her head into Mayer's and the American held her ground, pushing back before they ended up side-by-side and exchanging verbal insults.

"She isn't intimidating me," Cameron said after security stepped in. "All that yapping and getting in my face - just watch tomorrow."

Mayer, 36, claimed Cameron, 35, had said she would be "too slow", something the WBO champion dismissed.

"That's in your head, you're deluded. Shut your mouth, you're so deluded and you're making things up because you don't believe in yourself," Cameron responded.

After being pulled apart for a second time, Mayer added: "I didn't know this Cameron existed, she's going to need it."

Mayer and Cameron both came in 6lb shy of the light-middleweight limit at 10st 8lb (67kg).

Former undisputed light-welterweight champion Cameron has won 22 of her 23 fights as a professional, with her only defeat coming in a rematch with Katie Taylor in 2023.

Mayer is a three-weight world champion with 22 victories from 24 contests - losing to Briton Natasha Jonas and fellow American Alycia Baumgardner.

There was also plenty of tension when WBC and WBO lightweight champion Caroline Dubois and Amelia Moore faced off before their co-main event bout.

Dubois rolled her eyes and laughed during Thursday's news conference when Moore, who has only fought four times as a professional, said she had the tools to hand a first defeat to the Briton.

Both smiled as they were nose-to-nose on Friday with Dubois making her intentions clear as the weigh-in host placed a microphone between them.

"I told her I'm coming to take her head off," Dubois said.

Despite lacking experience in the professional ranks, 36-year-old Moore enjoyed a long amateur career and went through three Olympic cycles with the USA.

"It's very generic, she is saying the same thing to me that she's says to everyone," Moore said.

"It's a fight, Caroline. Welcome to the game. This is my world, I've been here a long time."

Moore tipped the scales at 9st 8lb (61kg) with Dubois one pound heavier as she looks to extend her unbeaten record to 15, having won 13 and drawn one.

title: Hovland in tie for lead at Tour Championship
description: Norway's Viktor Hovland and American Ryan Gerard in tie for the lead at 10 under, heading into the weekend at the Tour Championship in Atlanta.
fullText:
-10 R Gerard (US), V Hovland (Nor); -9 C Morikawa (US), C Gotterup (US); -8 S Scheffler (US), C Young (US)

Selected others: -7 M Fitzpatrick (Eng), J Rose (Eng), A Scott (Aus), L Aberg (Swe); R -6 Fox (NZ); -4 T Fleetwood (Eng), A Fitzpatrick (Eng), W Clark (US); -3 R McIlroy (NI); +3 R MacIntyre (Sco)

Norway's Viktor Hovland and American Ryan Gerard are tied for the lead at 10 under, heading into the weekend at the Tour Championship in Atlanta.

Hovland, who was crowned the Fedex Cup champion in 2023, made a birdie on the final hole to card a four-under 66, after Gerard had set the clubhouse pace with a five-under 65.

While Hovland's putting again came to the fore, Gerard was not to be outdone and memorably rolled in a stunning 78-foot birdie putt that travelled the length of the seventh green.

Collin Morikawa and Chris Gotterup are joint-second on nine under, while world number one Scottie Scheffler shrugged off two early bogeys to fire a 67, leaving him just two shots back in the PGA Tour's season-ending event.

Cameron Young, who won the Players Championship in March, is also at eight under after a scintillating round of 62 that contained seven birdies and an eagle on the par-five 18th.

England's Justin Rose and Matt Fitzpatrick are also firmly in contention to take home the $10m (£7.4m) prize on Sunday evening and are three strokes adrift at seven under overall.

Rose looked in superb form as he delivered a bogey-free 65, however, it was another day of mixed fortunes for Rory McIlroy who opened with a birdie but found himself two-over par after four holes.

The Northern Irishman's frustration was evident on the third hole, when he missed the green with his approach and then twice failed to chip his ball on to the putting surface from the same spot on his way to a double bogey.

And while he made two birdies in the final three holes, the Masters champion will need to make significant headway on Saturday, from his current position - tied for 23rd on three under.

Scotland's Robert MacIntyre also had a forgettable day, particularly after the turn.

The 30-year-old followed three consecutive bogeys with a double bogey on the par-three 15th hole after finding the water off the tee.

He eventually signed for a six-over 76 and alongside Min Woo Lee and Xander Schauffele, was one of only three players to conclude his second round over par.

However, his route to a bogey on the 18th was far from as unusual as the one taken by Jacob Bridgeman, whose stray tee shot landed inside a stall selling pizza.

title: McInnes backs himself to deliver Rangers success
description: Manager Derek McInnes says Rangers are "a long way away" from what he wants but backs himself to deliver success at Ibrox.
fullText:
Manager Derek McInnes says Rangers are "a long way away" from what he wants but backs himself to deliver success at Ibrox.

The 55-year-old oversaw a second exit from European competition this season with a Conference League play-off defeat on penalties by Czech side Jablonec.

Domestically, Rangers have progressed in the League Cup and will host Celtic in the quarter-finals next month but McInnes' side have picked up just one point from their opening two Scottish Premiership matches and visit Aberdeen on Sunday.

"I like to think I know what I'm doing as a manager, I'm a good manager, I back myself but at the minute, none of us are doing our job well enough," McInnes told Sky Sports.

"The players need a wee bit of help and support at the minute.

"We're a long way away from the Rangers team that I want us to be and the Rangers team that I intend us to be. The players are working extremely hard.

"There's a lot of uncertainty at the minute. Once the window closes, everything becomes a bit calmer."

Rangers to give Celtic 300 tickets for cup game

Rangers count consequences of European failure

Twelve players have been recruited already and McInnes hopes to sign "a couple more" and expects "one or two" to leave before the closure of the transfer window next week.

"We're not quite there," McInnes said.

"We've obviously missed big Youssef [Chermiti, who is injured], the type of striker to go and stretch teams.

"I don't expect us to be perfect at this stage. It's not been the start we wanted, I'm not the first Rangers manager to get off to a tough start but we are determined to follow this job through and it's the end that counts and I still believe we're going to be a success here."

After Thursday's match, McInnes lamented his side's struggle to be either possession-based, counter attacking or direct.

"My teams have always had some sort of identity," explained the former Aberdeen, Hearts, Kilmarnock and St Johnstone manager.

"I want us to try and be a team that puts more stress on teams defensively and I don't think that we are at the minute.

"We've got good ball players and I think we just need to relax a wee bit 

"I want us to be able to be a team that goes full press but when you go full press and you're aggressive, you've got to be really aggressive with that and you've got to pick up second balls and win duels and turn the ball over and really impose yourself on the game.

"There's talented players here. You don't get in the door at Rangers unless you're a talented player."

title: Greaves loses thriller to Cross on European debut
description: Beau Greaves narrowly loses 6-5 to Rob Cross on her European Tour debut in the Hungarian Darts Trophy.
fullText:
Beau Greaves narrowly lost 6-5 to Rob Cross on her European Tour debut in the Hungarian Darts Trophy.

The 22-year-old beat Tom Bissell last month to become the first woman to qualify for a PDC European Tour event.

England's Cross won the opening leg in Budapest before Greaves took a 2-1 lead in a thrilling encounter.

They continued exchanging legs as Greaves went 5-4 up to close in on becoming the first women to win a European Tour match.

Requiring 70 to win the match in the deciding leg, Greaves made two poor errors and was punished by Cross.

The narrow defeat continues a remarkable rise after she became the first woman to win a PDC ranking title in April.

Luke Humphries and Michael van Gerwen will enter the tournament in the second round, while world champion Luke Littler is not playing.

title: 'I learned from Murray' - Boulter won't make wedding ring mistake
description: Andy Murray has long been a guiding figure for British tennis, but newly-married Katie Boulter will not be following his lead when it comes to keeping her wedding ring safe as she prepares for the US Open.
fullText:
Andy Murray has long been a guiding figure for British tennis, but newly-married Katie Boulter will not be following his lead when it comes to keeping her wedding ring safe.

Three-time Grand Slam champion Murray, who married wife Kim in 2015, famously briefly lost his wedding band after playing with it tied to his shoe laces.

Murray had left his trainers - with the ring still attached - under a car to dry out after a practice session in California in 2021, and after discovering they were missing the next day, was eventually reunited with both after putting out an appeal for their return.

Boulter, who married Australia's world number seven Alex de Minaur this summer, said she will not be making the same mistake.

"I learned from Andy. I'm not going to do that," the 30-year-old said. "I don't wear it. Not during matches."

Boulter and De Minaur tied the knot at a small, private ceremony in England before holding a bigger celebration in Tuscany, Italy, in July.

Speaking to BBC Sport, Boulter said: "One was in the UK for my nearest and dearest. It was like eight people - very, very small, very much for my grandpa.

"It was a huge contrast to the Italian wedding, which had all of our closest people, all of our friends, and was a little bit more of a party and a lot of fun."

When it came to De Minaur's speech, however, Boulter admitted she was "sceptical".

"I hadn't seen him do any preparation for the speech at all. And he was like, 'I'm just going to wing it. It's fine. How hard can it be?'," she said.

"He was amazing. He was so, good. I was crying the whole time. I think I permanently cried for like three hours straight during all the speeches."

Since their wedding, the world number 60 has wasted no time in throwing herself back into tennis before the US Open, which gets under way on Sunday.

"I actually just chose to go straight back into the conditions, go into the deep end and see what we've got," said Boulter, who lost in the first round in Washington and Toronto before suffering a second-round exit in Cincinnati.

"I do think the conditions in the States are very different from the UK. I think you can't really replicate them.

"So I felt like I'd be a little underprepared coming to the US and just getting used to the conditions again would have been quite difficult."

Boulter's US Open begins with a first-round encounter against American wildcard Carol Young Suh Lee, who is ranked 143rd in the world.

How to follow US Open on the BBC

A record four British players have made it through qualifying to reach the main draw at the US Open.

Fran Jones, Harriet Dart and Harry Wendelken all won their third and final qualifying matches on Friday, while Toby Samuel advanced on Thursday after his opponent, Chile's Cristian Garin, retired during a lengthy rain delay.

It is the first time that four British players have progressed from qualifying at an overseas Grand Slam since the Australian Open of 1988.

Jacob Fearnley lost to Austria's Jurij Rodionov in a rain-disrupted match that stretched across Thursday and Friday, but the 25-year-old will play Spain's Martin Landaluce in the first round after securing a main draw spot as a lucky loser.

The five Britons will join compatriots Arthur Fery, Cameron Norrie, Jan Choinski and Boulter in the main draws.

Wendelken earned his first appearance in the main draw at an overseas Grand Slam as he fought back to beat Lithuania's Vilius Gaubas 6-7 (3-7) 7-6 (7-5) 7-6 (10-5).

He will face Italian 22nd seed Luciano Darderi in the first round, while Samuel is up against the Czech Republic's Tomas Machac.

Jones, meanwhile, claimed a straightforward 6-4 6-1 win over Taiwan's Joanna Garland to qualify for a second successive year and set up a first-round meeting with Poland's Magda Linette

Meanwhile, Heather Watson missed out on her first US Open singles main-draw appearance in five years as Dart fought back from a set and a break down to win 2-6 6-4 6-1.

"It's never easy playing against a friend and Heather is such an a great player and has so much experience," Dart told BBC Sport.

"It showed for an hour and a half, I was really behind and she was playing some really good tennis. In the end I was able to stick to it somehow and find a way and turn it in my favour."

Dart, who has reached the second round in her last two main draw appearances at Flushing Meadows, will play American Peyton Stearns in the first round.

title: Leeds go back top with thumping win at St Helens
description: Leeds Rhinos go back to the top of the Super League standings on points difference with a rare and comprehensive away win at St Helens.
fullText:
Tries: Hankinson, Smith, Newman, Hall, Handley, Croft Goals: Connor 5

Leeds Rhinos moved back to the top of Super League on points difference with a rare and comprehensive away win at St Helens.

The Rhinos' first win at Saints since March 2023 means they will secure their first League Leaders' Shield for 11 years if they beat second-placed Wigan in a decider for the trophy next Saturday.

Cameron Smith scored the pick of the Rhinos' six tries on the night with a stunning individual effort as they raced into a commanding 18-point lead at the break.

Defeat for St Helens signals a damaging blow to their hopes of making this season's play-offs, failing to capitalise on Hull KR's heavy defeat last night by Wigan, staying two points below the sixth-placed Robins with two games remaining.

Huddersfield upset Leigh with five-try win

Catalans beat Cas in game halted by power outage

After an impeccably observed minute's silence in honour of the late Sir Billy Boston by everyone inside the Brewdog Stadium, an incisive dash and short ball from Jake Connor allowed Chris Hankinson to crash over from close range to break the deadlock.

Leeds momentarily thought they had scored a second try in two minutes as Cooper Jenkins went over under the sticks but Brodie Croft was penalised for a forward pass when attempting to knock the ball backwards.

While down to 12 men because of Daniel Suluka-Fifita's hit on Presley Cassell off the ball, Saints thought they were over but Tristan Sailor's lofted pass to Deon Cross was spotted to be forward as the winger dived in at the left corner.

Second-rower Smith then broke a tackle from Suluka-Fifita, back on the field, and gave the Saints backline a clean set of heels before getting down low to finish off an outstanding individual score.

The match was effectively taken away from Saints when slick hands from Connor set up Ash Handley who in turn found Harry Newman to dive over unopposed as Connor slotted the extras to give Leeds an 18-point lead at the break.

Tom Holroyd had a try disallowed a minute after half-time, unable to ground the ball before knocking on under pressure from Saints full-back Sailor.

Leeds did get their fourth try soon after though when Jack Bird's beautiful backhanded offload freed up Ryan Hall to dot down his 357th career try.

Saints were on the board when Jack Welsby's line break saw him race clear of Leeds' midfield and full-back Lachie Miller for the match's second excellent individual try.

But that proved to be just brief respite as Handley got on the scoresheet, latching on to a grubber kick from Connor, and another grubber from Connor found his half-back partner Croft, via the upright, for his 28th Super League try of the season.

Connor missed a penalty late on, striking the post, but his kicking game continues to impress with Leeds looking strong going into the upcoming play-offs.

Saints, meanwhile, will have to beat Leigh and Hull KR in their final two matches if they are to avoid missing out on the Super League play-offs for the first time.

Leeds Rhinos coach Brad Arthur told BBC Radio Leeds:

"I thought both our starts to the first half and the second half were pretty good. We did it with a good control.

"We had to stay composed and that was a good test for us. We had players all over the shop the last 15 minutes but they still had a pride in their defence which has been a bit questionable at times this season.

"If we can withstand the pressure for three, four sets, which we're going to have to do against Wigan next week, it can take a bit of confidence out of your opposition.

"We're up against a really good team who have been at the top of their game for a long, long time. So we're excited, we've done the work, now we've got to be confident."

title: Haaland and Cherki fire impressive Man City to victory at Palace
description: Erling Haaland and Rayan Cherki both score twice as Manchester City cruise to a 4-1 win at Crystal Palace in the Premier League.
fullText: Haaland and Cherki fire impressive Man City to victory at PalaceThis content is not available in your location.There was an errorErling Haaland and Rayan Cherki both score twice as Manchester City cruise to a 4-1 win at Crystal Palace in the Premier League.

title: A magician and a maverick - this could be Cherki's moment for Man City
description: After two goals and a swaggering display against Crystal Palace, Phil McNulty asks if this is Rayan Cherki's time to shine for Manchester City.
fullText:
Rayan Cherki refuses to hide his emotions, an open book for all to see and hear in times of joy and disappointment.

Moments after Manchester City had put down their first heavyweight marker of the post-Pep Guardiola era by brushing aside Crystal Palace, he was asked live on TV how much he enjoyed the game. Rather than providing the usual textbook answer, he instead gave a colourfully uncomplimentary – and unprintable - description of his own first-half performance.

Erling Haaland, standing alongside Cherki as he waited to hand over the player-of-the-match award, could only laugh at the France attacker's sweary honesty.

Indeed, the 23-year-old also refuses to hide his talent, making a nonsense of his self-criticism by unveiling a Selhurst Park masterclass with two brilliant second-half goals in the 4-1 victory.

Cherki made his impact under Guardiola last season, although there was always a feeling the mercurial signing from Lyon for a bargain £30m could produce more. He made 33 Premier League appearances - but 14 of those were as a substitute.

And there is a sense that he already has something to prove under new boss Enzo Maresca amid City's vast attacking resources, coming off the bench to assist the two late goals that gave them victory against Bournemouth on the opening weekend.

Cherki was seen in animated conversation with Maresca after the final whistle, but his reward was a start at Selhurst Park and he delivered the sort of irresistible performance he, as well as City, needed.

Cherki inspires Man City to comfortable win at Palace

Cherki genius and Wharton excels - Palace v Man City player ratings

He had a disappointing World Cup with France, reduced to a bit-part player, only starting against England in the third-fourth place play-off, being replaced at half-time with his side 4-0 down.

There were also videos that emerged with Cherki showing apparent displeasure at coach Didier Deschamps.

Cherki has a reputation for unpredictability, with Maresca saying after his contribution against Bournemouth that "if he is not happy he wants to show it".

But, though he has proved hard to please in the past at Leicester City and Chelsea, Maresca was satisfied with Cherki here.

"He's happy and I'm happy," said Maresca. "It was not just his performance with the two goals, but his work off the ball.

"He pressed and gave us a complete performance on the ball and off the ball.

"Rayan is Rayan. We know him. He loves football and it makes it so much easier to work with him.

"The quality he has in this moment helps the team, not just with assists but goals."

It was not just Cherki's wizardry with the ball that impressed Maresca, but his work off it.

"His performance off the ball was unbelievable," he added to BBC Match of the Day. "Everyone knows his quality but when he works hard off the ball, he was in charge of Adam Wharton. He controlled him. He was very good."

Praise indeed as the outstanding Wharton is one of the players City have cast their eyes over as they try to strengthen Maresca's squad before the close of the transfer window.

For all the team work that brought such praise from Maresca, it was the two moments of individual genius that will be remembered after a win and performance that suggested talk that City will inevitably go into decline after the departure of Guardiola has been greatly exaggerated.

He also produced those defining moments at crucial times, the first coming nine minutes into the second half with City leading 1-0 and Palace hoping to mount a recovery.

Cherki took Phil Foden's pass on the edge of the area, embarking on a slalom run surrounded by four Palace defenders, leaving them helpless before poking a left-foot finish past keeper Dean Henderson.

He celebrated with a touch of arrogance that is so often the preserve of the special ones, staring down the Palace fans on the Holmesdale Road end.

And after Palace pulled one back, it was Cherki who once again restored that two-goal advantage with a rising right-foot shot from 20 yards past Henderson.

Former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp told Sky Sports: "After Rayan Cherki painted a masterpiece, City started to play and got a real hold of it.

"Cherki felt like the difference because his goals came at an important time. He is a genius. The things he can do with a football are absolute genius.

"There aren't many Premier League players I've seen that can do this on the first goal.

"Eden Hazard possibly, he was that kind of player. Georgi Kinkladze, there'll be Manchester City fans from a previous generation who'll remember him, who could get past people in a telephone box. This was very similar.

"Once Cherki is in the box, they are so scared to touch him. It's absolute genius. He's an absolute bargain at £30m and gives you a new dimension. He gives you that 'X-factor'. He does things differently.

Cherki's goal celebrations summed up his confidence and attitude, with Redknapp saying: "There was a bit of Cantona about him. He's a beautiful player. With someone like Cherki you've got to let him do his thing."

There may be ups and downs between the maverick Cherki and the demanding Maresca, but the France star with stardust in his boots showed he will not be pushed to the back of the queue among City's array of attacking talent – with perhaps more to come before the deadline.

And that is good news for Maresca as he tried to build on the foundations left behind by Guardiola.
